havenco.story:
HavenCo was an internet hosting company that operated from Sealand, a Second World War sea fort in the North Sea, about seven miles off the English coast. The fort's occupants, the Bates family, have called it an independent country since 1967. A hosting company keeps computers connected to the internet and rents space on them to customers who run websites or store records. HavenCo's selling point was the location. It was meant to be a data haven, the information version of a tax haven, a place where data that was illegal or could be seized elsewhere would sit out of reach of other countries' courts.

The idea came from a group of American programmers known as cypherpunks, who believed that encryption and free flow of information could protect people from government power. Sean Hastings, who had moved to the Caribbean island of Anguilla to work on online gambling, met Ryan Lackey, a college dropout from MIT, at a conference there in 1998. Hastings decided Anguilla would not work, because gambling and pornography were illegal there and a court could close a company. They read Erwin Strauss's book How to Start Your Own Country and settled on Sealand. Avi Freedman and Joichi Ito came in as investors.

The plan gave the Bates family and advisers a third of the company and hoped for a stock market listing worth $500 million. HavenCo promised customers first-world infrastructure with third-world regulation. It expected a typical customer to be a firm wanting records a court order could not reach. Publicity described machine rooms flooded with nitrogen so that intruders would need scuba gear. If Britain ever forced the issue, the founders told investors, the fallback was to accept British law and run as an ordinary British hosting site. Michael Bates bought a dormant British company in August 2000 and renamed it HavenCo Limited, and the business was also incorporated in Anguilla and later in Cyprus.

Launched in 2000 with a Wired magazine cover story, it delivered much less. The nitrogen was never installed, and the south tower was never full of servers. The cable to England was late, and the firm supplying it went bankrupt in the dot-com crash, which caused a two-month outage. The backup satellite link ran at about the speed of a good home connection. It had about ten customers, most of them gambling sites, and it only broke even on day-to-day cash costs. Hastings and his wife Jo left by the end of summer 2000.

The larger problem was the host. HavenCo owed Sealand large scheduled payments that assumed fast profits. An adviser to the Bates family began to interfere in technical decisions. In May 2002 the family refused a plan to stream films, fearing American pressure on Britain, and Lackey decided to leave. In November 2002 Sealand offered to take over the company on agreed terms that would pay its debts and issue shares. Lackey handed over access to the servers and said the terms were broken within days, so the company had been, in his words, probably effectively nationalized, meaning taken over by the state.

He had no remedy. Sealand's monarch headed its courts, and going to a court anywhere else would have conceded that other countries had power over what happened on Sealand, which was the opposite of what the business sold. The new management barred anything against international law. The website went offline in 2008. In 2013 Freedman announced a revival using servers in the European Union and the United States, with some stored data kept on Sealand. It is not known to have succeeded.

James Grimmelmann, the law professor who wrote the fullest history, argued that HavenCo failed from too little law. It escaped British courts and so had no neutral court to protect it from the family who controlled its building, its power and its computers.

knock-john-radio-essex.story:
Knock John is one of four naval sea forts Britain built in the outer Thames Estuary during the Second World War to defend the approaches to London against aircraft. It stands on legs on a sandbank about 16 kilometres off the Essex coast. It was grounded in August 1942, left in 1945 and abandoned altogether in 1956. To anyone looking from a boat it appeared to be far out to sea, and that appearance turned out to matter in court.

In the mid-1960s the BBC held a legal monopoly on radio in Britain and played far less pop and rock music than many listeners wanted. Anyone else broadcasting to the public could be prosecuted, but British law on land stopped at the territorial sea, the belt of coastal water a state fully controls, which then ran three miles. Entrepreneurs therefore began broadcasting from ships and abandoned forts beyond that limit, and they sold advertising. Roy Bates, a former army major who had built up factories and a fishing fleet after the war, joined them in 1965. He set up Radio Essex on Knock John after driving off staff of the rival station Radio City. The station was later renamed Britain's Better Music Station.

The legal question was where the three miles start. The limit is not measured from whatever beach is nearest. It runs from a baseline, a line fixed by law, and bays and estuaries on the landward side of that line count as internal waters. A fort can be many kilometres from the shore and still be inside. Knock John sat in the mouth of a wide estuary, so the measured line ran well outside it.

For a while this hardly mattered, because the government left the stations alone. That changed after one radio entrepreneur shot another in June 1966. Bates received a summons in September 1966 under the Wireless Telegraphy Act, which banned unlicensed broadcasting, and government files recorded interference from his station as far away as Hungary. On 30 November magistrates found him guilty and fined him £100. He appealed, arguing that the fort lay outside the limit. In January 1967 the Essex Quarter Sessions, a local court, held that Knock John lay a little over a mile and a half on the up-river side of the measured line, and so inside internal waters. The Post Office then spent months trying to collect its costs from him.

Bates had already shut the station on Christmas Day 1966. He moved his equipment to Roughs Tower, the fort farthest out to sea, which was beyond the limit however it was measured. He never resumed broadcasting there, and in September 1967 he declared it the Principality of Sealand. Knock John itself was left empty and still stands, slightly distorted, according to a 2009 observation.

The case shows why anyone hoping to escape a country's law at sea has to work from the legal chart and not from the distance to the beach.
knock-john-radio-essex.why: Corrected the wording on distance. The court's finding, as quoted in Grimmelmann's footnote 51, was that the fort lay a little over a mile and a half on the up-river side of the measured line, which is not the same as that distance from the coast.

radio-390-red-sands.story:
Red Sands is a group of steel towers on legs in the Thames Estuary, near Whitstable in Kent, built during the Second World War as an army anti-aircraft fort and later abandoned. Forts like this were cheaper for pirate broadcasters than buying a ship, and in the 1960s several were taken over for unlicensed radio. Pirate radio existed because the BBC held a legal monopoly on British broadcasting. A station could hope to avoid prosecution only if it stood outside the three-mile territorial limit, the belt of sea a state then fully controlled.

Two weak stations used Red Sands first. Radio Invicta began in 1964, and its owner, a local fisherman, drowned that December with two colleagues when their small boat overturned in a squall on the way back to shore. Supplies ran so low the next month that the station sent out distress calls. It closed and became K-I-N-G Radio, which also failed to pay its way and approached Ted Allbeury for help. Allbeury suggested programmes modelled on women's magazines and aimed at people at home during the day. Radio 390, named after a wavelength close to its real one, started in 1965 with easy-listening music. A rival mocked it as Stone Age radio, but it became popular. The fort itself gave it a technical advantage. A 250-foot mast on an inner tower, held by cables from the outer towers, gave a 10-kilowatt transmitter good coverage of southern England, although the station told advertisers it had 35 kilowatts.

Its legal trouble came with the wider crackdown of 1966. On 25 November a magistrates' court convicted its managers of illegal broadcasting, fined them £100 and ordered the station closed. They appealed, and in December the High Court decided the case, R v Kent Justices ex parte Lye, by two judges to one. The question was where to begin measuring the three miles. A government order of 1964 allowed measurement from a low-tide elevation, a sandbank that shows only at low water. Measured from such a bank, the fort was inside the limit. The fort stayed where it was, and the legal line moved past it.

This ruling matters to anyone trying to build offshore. The location of a structure can be correct on the day it is occupied and wrong after a government changes how the line is drawn, or after a court reads an old order in a new way. Radio 390 returned on 31 December with fresh evidence that the fort lay outside the limit. Magistrates rejected that evidence in February 1967 and fined the company £200 and its directors £40 each. The station carried on. The Post Office then used a different tool, a civil court order called an injunction, which it won in May.

An appeal was refused on 28 July, because Parliament had by then passed the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act. That law made it an offence for British citizens to take part in offshore broadcasts or to supply or advertise on them, so the location of the fort no longer decided anything. It would have closed the station by 14 August in any case. Radio 390 went off the air that day with the national anthem. Thieves raided the empty fort a week later and were arrested soon after.
radio-390-red-sands.mechanism: The court in R v Kent Justices held that a sandbank visible only at low tide can move the starting line for measuring the territorial sea outward, which brought an offshore fort inside national law without the fort moving. Parliament then closed the remaining gap with a law aimed at the people and businesses behind the stations, wherever the stations stood.

radio-city-shivering-sands.story:
Shivering Sands is an abandoned Second World War army fort in the Thames Estuary off England, a cluster of steel towers on legs that once stood seven strong. One tower was knocked down when a ship hit it, and another was left isolated. In the 1960s it housed Radio City, one of the unlicensed stations that broadcast pop music to Britain from just offshore, because the BBC held a monopoly on legal radio and played little of it.

The musician Screaming Lord Sutch started the station as Radio Sutch on 27 May 1964. It was a low-budget affair, with a transmitter from a Halifax bomber, car batteries for power and a scaffold pole with a skull-and-crossbones flag as an aerial. By September Sutch had tired of it and sold it to his friend and unpaid manager, Reginald Calvert, for a reported £5,000. Calvert repaired the catwalks between the towers, fixed up living quarters, built studios, and raised a tall mast on the central tower. Output never exceeded 2 kilowatts, though the station claimed 10 to attract advertisers. Part of its income came from Dutch and American religious shows that paid for airtime. The Port of London Authority complained that its signal interfered with radio links to wind and tide gauges on the isolated tower, which could put shipping at risk.

Possession of the fort depended largely on who was physically there. In September 1965 Radio City began merger talks with Radio Caroline, and a transmitter was delivered to the fort for Caroline's use. Major Oliver Smedley, a retired officer behind another station, claimed to own it. The transmitter proved unusable, the merger collapsed and nobody collected it. Calvert then explored a merger with Radio London. At 3 a.m. on 20 June 1966 seamen sent by Smedley boarded the fort and took it from the disc jockeys, intending to hold it for ransom. The next evening he went to Smedley's home and was shot dead there. Smedley was charged with murder and cleared on grounds of self-defence.

The shooting was widely reported. Law professor James Grimmelmann's history says it turned public feeling against the stations and led the government to step up enforcement of the Wireless Telegraphy Act, which banned unlicensed broadcasting. It also led toward the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act of 1967. Other stations, including Roy Bates's Radio Essex, were prosecuted that autumn. It was then established, following a new reading of the rules on territorial waters, that Shivering Sands itself lay inside British waters, so existing law covered it. Radio City closed at midnight on 8 February 1967, and the national anthem was its last broadcast.

Grimmelmann also notes that Bates was linked in a vague way to a plan to seize Shivering Sands in the winter of 1967, which may have been a hoax. The case shows how a dispute over an offshore structure could turn violent when no police were on hand.
radio-city-shivering-sands.mechanism: Offshore forts were lightly policed until a killing over one of them made the issue political. The government then applied broadcasting law to the forts and found, on a new reading of the rules, that this fort had been inside British waters.

rem-island.story:
REM Island is a steel platform built in 1964 to broadcast commercial radio and television to the Netherlands from the North Sea. At that time the Dutch had one television channel, with airtime divided among six public broadcasting groups, and advertising on it was strictly forbidden. Advertisers and viewers both wanted something else, and pirate stations on ships were already reaching several North Sea countries. REM, short for Reclame Exploitatie Maatschappij, or Advertising Operation Company, saw a market.

The company did something new. Earlier European pirates had used ships, or old military structures in Britain's case, and REM had a platform built for the purpose in the harbour of Cork, Ireland. It was towed to a spot about 10 kilometres off Noordwijk and anchored in cement on the seabed. Test broadcasts began in August 1964, and regular television started on 1 September at 6:30 in the evening with an advertisement for Johnson's Pledge furniture polish. The money came from advertising, some of it collected before the station even existed. Commercials were shot on 16mm film and spliced into imported series such as The Saint, Mister Ed and The Adventures of Robin Hood before the reels were sent out to the platform. Viewers needed a special aerial, and the station aimed at about 750,000 sets in the western Netherlands. A survey that August found 83 per cent of respondents against closing it.

Dutch law banned such broadcasts. The platform stood outside territorial waters, the coastal belt a state fully controls, so officials had no power to stop it there. The government's answer relied on a newer idea in the law of the sea, the 1958 Geneva Convention, which gave a coastal state rights over the continental shelf, the seabed off its coast. The Senate passed a law on 1 December 1964 forbidding the platform's radio and television services, and on 12 December the government put into effect a measure that divided the North Sea into national sections and declared the seabed under the structure to be Dutch territory. A platform anchored to that seabed was now treated as standing on the Netherlands. The stations went silent. Five days later Dutch marines boarded the platform.

This is the important difference from a ship. A ship can be moved and answers to the country whose flag it flies. Something fixed to the seabed can be reached by claiming the seabed.

The backers formed a new company, TROS, in a final effort to survive, and a year later it came back legally as a public broadcaster. Television advertising was legalised in the Netherlands in 1967. The government used the platform to measure sea temperature and salt levels. A sale attempt failed in 2004, and it was dismantled in 2006. Since March 2011 it has stood in Amsterdam's harbour as a restaurant.
rem-island.mechanism: A state can reach a structure beyond its territorial sea by claiming the seabed the structure stands on. Anything fixed to that seabed then falls under the coastal state's law, which is why building a permanent platform gave REM less protection than a ship had.

rose-island.story:
The Republic of Rose Island was a platform in the Adriatic Sea, nearly 12 kilometres off Rimini, Italy, whose builder declared it an independent country. Italian territorial waters, the coastal belt a state fully controls, ended a few hundred metres short of it. Rimini is a beach resort, so summer tourists were close at hand.

Its builder was Giorgio Rosa, an engineer from Bologna who liked engineering experiments and disliked the bureaucracy around property. He had the idea in 1958 and spent about two years studying how to fix a structure to the seabed. His method, which he patented, was to build a frame on the beach, float it out, lower hollow pillars to the bottom, drive steel tubes through them into the sea floor and fill them with cement. The sea and weather allowed only a few working hours a week, so construction took years. The result was a 400-square-metre deck on nine pylons, with a well reaching fresh water 280 metres below the sea floor.

Late in 1966 the Rimini harbour office asked him to stop, partly because nearby areas had been leased to the state energy company ENI. Police also took an interest. He carried on and opened to the public in summer 1967, with a bar, restaurant, nightclub, shop and post office, and started a second storey. On 1 May 1968 he declared independence and made himself president. The state's official name was in Esperanto, the invented international language, and its government was made up of Rosa's relatives and acquaintances. Its currency, the mill, was set equal to the Italian lira, but no coins or notes are known, only stamps. It used an anthem from a Wagner opera. Nobody is known to have lived there apart from a guard and his partner.

He held a press conference in June. Italian officials suspected that the point was to take money from tourists without paying tax on it. Rosa met an official of the military intelligence service, with no result. On 26 June, 55 days after the declaration, police and tax officers came by boat, took control and blockaded the platform. Rosa telegraphed Italy's president, Giuseppe Saragat, and got no reply. Questions were asked in parliament, and he received several offers to buy the platform.

In August the merchant marine ministry ordered him to demolish it, and his appeal failed. Everything movable was taken ashore in November. The platform survived two explosive charges in February 1969, and a storm sank it on 26 February. Rosa issued stamps showing the destruction. He died in 2017, having approved a film about the episode, and Rose Island was released on Netflix in 2020.

The Council of State, Italy's top administrative court, held the claims of independence and sovereignty unfounded. Its reasoning turned on the person and not the place. Italian citizens remain subject to Italian law even outside Italy. Standing outside territorial waters therefore did not free an Italian who built, ran and profited from a platform there. For anyone planning something similar, this means that distance alone does not end the duties owed to the country of citizenship, and a platform close enough for tourists is close enough for police boats.

add_sources.t: Archeology of Rose Island, Space Caviar

sealand.story:
Sealand is a former British sea fort in the North Sea whose occupants have claimed since 1967 that it is an independent country. It is a 120-foot by 50-foot deck on two concrete legs, 60 feet above the water, built in 1942 as Roughs Tower, about 6 nautical miles off Suffolk and 7 off Essex. About 120 men lived in the legs during the war, and Britain then abandoned it. Because it stood more than three miles out, it was beyond Britain's territorial sea of the time, the coastal belt a state fully controls.

Roy Bates, a former army major, came to it through pirate radio. After a conviction for running a station on a fort inside the limit, he took Roughs Tower at the end of 1966 from Radio Caroline staff. His first occupation failed when his men ran short of food and a British lifeboat took them off. He retook it in April 1967 and fought off Radio Caroline with an air rifle and petrol bombs. Officials wanted the fort destroyed. The Ministry of Defence offered him £5,000 to leave, and he asked for £90,000. Government lawyers concluded that a civil action to recover the fort would probably fail. On 2 September 1967 he declared the Principality of Sealand, with himself as prince.

The key court case came next. In May 1968 his son Michael fired a pistol across the bow of a ship servicing a buoy, and both men were charged when they next came ashore. A judge at Chelmsford ruled that October that the firearms law did not apply, because Parliament had never extended it beyond the three-mile limit. The family treats this as recognition. It decided only how far one English statute reached, and British officials told their Belgian counterparts that it was not recognition. A meeting at the Cabinet Office that November concluded that Bates was doing no actual harm and that no force or special law was justified. British policy after that was that Sealand was outside the United Kingdom and also was not a state.

Life on the fort has been small. Coins dated from 1972 and stamps from 1969, but Sealand does not belong to the international postal union, so its stamps are not postage elsewhere. For long periods one or two people lived there, reached by a winch from a boat or by helipad, and its mailing address runs through a British postbag.

In 1978 a court in Cologne heard the case of Alexander Achenbach, a German who drafted Sealand's 1975 constitution and wanted to drop his German citizenship. Applying the usual test for a state, it held that Sealand had no real territory, population or effective government. That August Achenbach's lawyer, Gernot Pütz, took over the fort while the elder Bateses were lured to Austria. They retook it by helicopter, fined Pütz 75,000 Deutsche Marks and held him for about six weeks. A German diplomat came out to check on him, which the family cites as recognition, while Germany called the episode an act of piracy. In 1997 Sealand revoked all of its passports after a Madrid ring sold fakes.

On 1 October 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which covers the tower, and it has held since then that Sealand is under its jurisdiction, though it has never tested this by force. In a 2006 fire, an RAF helicopter took the only person aboard to hospital and rescue crews chose not to charge for their work. Roy Bates died in 2012. His son Michael lives in England, and the family sells noble titles and an online citizenship costing about $10 a month, while one caretaker lives on the fort. Britain has not tried to remove the occupants since declaring the tower inside its waters.

sunk-head-fort.story:
Sunk Head was a Royal Navy sea fort placed about 18 kilometres off the Essex coast on 1 June 1942. It was one of the four naval Maunsell forts, named after their designer Guy Maunsell, a set of concrete towers and decks sunk onto the seabed in the outer Thames Estuary to defend the approach to London against aircraft and to give radar coverage. The navy decommissioned it in June 1945 and maintained it until 1956, when it was abandoned.

The fort matters because of where it stood. Some of its sister forts turned out to be inside British waters once lawyers measured the three-mile territorial limit, the belt of sea a state then fully controlled. Sunk Head was clearly well outside, in the same position as the nearby Roughs Tower, where Roy Bates was then establishing what he called the Principality of Sealand. An empty structure beyond the limit worried the government because British broadcasting law might not reach it.

A small group of radio enthusiasts ran a station called Radio Tower from the fort for a few months, with little money and poor coverage. They also claimed they would provide television, though this was never credible. When the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act took effect on 14 August 1967, it banned British citizens from taking part in offshore broadcasts, but foreigners supplied from abroad could still have used an empty fort. Officials were by then having great difficulty with Bates. Lawyers had advised them that a civil action to recover Roughs Tower would likely fail, and sending in Royal Marines to remove a man already there raised hard legal questions. An empty fort raised no such questions, since no one needed to be removed first.

On 18 August 1967 a party of the 24th Field Squadron, Royal Engineers, the British army's construction and demolition specialists, boarded from the tug Collie. They weakened the structure with cutting torches and laid explosives, 3,200 pounds according to one account and 2,200 according to another in the same source. At 4:18 in the afternoon on 21 August they blew it up, destroying the superstructure and most of the legs above the waterline. Stumps about 20 feet high remain.

The contrast with Sealand, a few miles away, is direct. Britain demolished the fort that nobody was living on, and it left in place the one with a family on it who would not go.
sunk-head-fort.mechanism: A state that built a structure outside its own waters can demolish it while it stands empty, which leaves any later occupier with nothing to stand on. Once someone has moved in, removing them first raises legal problems that demolition alone does not.

add_sources.t: Grimmelmann, Sealand, HavenCo, and the Rule of Law, University of Illinois Law Review 2012

itu-haps-definition.story:
Radio signals cross borders, so countries need a shared rulebook on who may use which frequencies. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the United Nations agency in Geneva that deals with radio, keeps that rulebook, called the Radio Regulations. Paragraph 1.66A of those regulations defines a high-altitude platform station as a station on an object at an altitude of 20 to 50 kilometres and at a specified, nominal, fixed point relative to the Earth. In plain words, it is a radio transmitter on something that hangs high in the sky over one spot, doing some of the work of a satellite.

The word station is the important one. The definition exists so that makers of these craft can be given frequencies. It does not describe a place where anyone may live, and it says nothing about who owns the air at that height.

The height band sits above ordinary traffic. Airliners fly lower, and the top band of controlled airspace in the United States, called Class A, ends at 60,000 feet, about 18 kilometres. Projects aimed at this band include the Airbus Zephyr, a solar-powered drone with an endurance goal of 64 days, the BAE PHASA-35, the Kea Atmos Mk1 and the Stratobus airship. Google's Loon balloons also worked in the stratosphere until the project ended in 2021.

Which law governs this height is unsettled. A 2023 dissertation at the University of Pretoria described a lack of clarity about the rules for these craft, because they sit between air law, run by national aviation authorities and the International Civil Aviation Organization, and the space treaties. No treaty fixes where a country's airspace ends. Anyone hoping to found a place at 20 kilometres would find the ITU able to help with a radio licence only, and that licence is applied for through a national government.
itu-haps-definition.mechanism: This is a radio rule and says nothing about who owns the air at 20 to 50 kilometres. Having a place in the radio regulations gives a platform a claim on frequencies and no claim to territory.

add_sources.t: High Altitude Platform Stations (HAPS): The new Frontier at the intersection between Air and Space Law, Coetzee, University of Pretoria, 2023

sky-cruise.story:
Sky Cruise is an idea for a giant nuclear-powered flying hotel, shown in an animated video that Hashem Al-Ghaili released in mid-2022. The original design came from an art director, Tony Holmsten, who drew it over a decade earlier. It exists only as images, and no base, company or site has been named, so it has no place on the ground.

The video shows a craft carrying up to 5,000 people and staying in the air for years, with passengers and supplies arriving on commercial and private jets that land on it. Al-Ghaili suggested that small nuclear reactors expected in the 2030s might power it. Viewers questioned its aerodynamics and whether it could fly at all, and Al-Ghaili himself stressed that it is only a concept. The project is on the map as the best-known image of a home that never touches land.

Staying in the air would not take it outside national law. Under the Chicago Convention, the main treaty on civil flying, an aircraft has the nationality of the country that registers it, and every jet shuttling people to it would have to leave from a licensed airport in some country. Whether any regulator would certify such a craft is unknown, because none has been asked. No such aircraft has been built.

add_sources.t: Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation, Wikipedia

sky-cruise.mechanism: An aircraft that never landed would still depend on jets flying from licensed airports, and it would still need a country of registration, whose law would travel with it.

stratobus.story:
Stratobus is a robotic airship designed to hover about 20 kilometres above the ground, above the jet stream and regular air traffic. It is on the map because it is one of the most developed plans for a large craft that stays in one spot in the stratosphere for years, the kind of object people picture when they talk about platforms in the sky. It has no people on board and none are planned. The developer is the French space company Thales Alenia Space, based in Cannes.

The attraction is cost and position. A satellite must keep moving around the Earth or sit very high above it, while an airship can stay over one area, close enough for sharp cameras and strong radio links. In 2015 the company's programme head described uses such as watching borders, spotting suspicious boats at 200 kilometres, restoring telephone links after disasters and bringing internet to remote areas. The French Ministry of Industry selected the idea for a national programme, and the design then was 100 metres long, about 5 tons, carrying up to 250 kilograms of equipment for five years, with a couple of days a year on the ground for maintenance. Solar cells charge a fuel cell, which keeps two motors running through the night to hold the craft against the wind. It could take off from an area the size of a football field and climb in under four hours.

The schedule kept slipping. Thales planned a prototype in 2018 or 2019 and commercial sale around 2020. In January 2020 the defence publisher Janes reported a French defence study of a surveillance version 115 metres long and nearly 7 tonnes, with flights planned by the end of 2023. In September 2025 Reuters quoted the head of Stratobus, Yannick Combet, describing a balloon 142 metres long, with the aim of being ready for use by 2031, and Aviation Week reported that the company had started building two reduced-scale test models.

The same Reuters report shows the reason for the new interest. The United States shot down a suspected Chinese balloon in 2023, and France published a strategy in 2025 for operating between 20 and 100 kilometres and downed two balloons as a demonstration. Combet said of the height band that it is a space that is not occupied. Reuters described it as a regulatory grey zone. In practice governments are still in control from the start. Thales said flight tests had to come before certification and flight authorisation, and these come from a national authority before the craft leaves the ground.
stratobus.mechanism: The airship needs certification and flight authorisation before it can fly, so a government controls it from the start, long before anyone asks who governs the air at that height. The main customers in view are also governments.

add_sources.t: France launches concept study for a Stratobus type HAPS, Janes, 15 Jan 2020

adiz-high-seas.story:
An air defense identification zone, usually shortened to ADIZ, is a stretch of sky in which a country, by its own declaration, requires aircraft to identify themselves and report where they are going. The zone may run far beyond that country's own airspace, which ends at the edge of its territorial sea, the coastal belt it fully controls. Beyond that belt is international airspace, where the 1982 law of the sea treaty gives every country freedom to fly. The purpose is time. A fast aircraft crosses a 12-mile belt in moments, so a government that wants warning has to ask questions earlier.

The United States created the first zone on 27 December 1950, during the Korean War, out of fear of a Soviet bomber attack. Under its law no one could fly in the zone without filing a flight plan, and foreign civil pilots heading for the country had to report their position one to two hours out. If radio questioning failed to identify an aircraft, the Air Force sent fighters to take a look. Canada's rules of 1951 went further and warned of interception. About 20 countries and regions now have such zones, including India, Japan, Australia and the United Kingdom.

No treaty creates them. They rest on each country's own rule and on what others tolerate. The American position is that the legal basis is a country's right to set reasonable conditions of entry to its territory, so its zone applies to commercial aircraft intending to enter American airspace. Robert Beckman of the National University of Singapore noted in 2014 that global conventions do not expressly forbid the zones, while freedom of overflight remains the overriding rule, and that many countries appear to apply their rules to any aircraft passing through. One view among legal writers is that declaring a zone breaks no law. Another says the zones conflict with freedom of navigation.

The sharpest test came on 23 November 2013, when China declared a zone over the East China Sea. It imposed reporting duties on aircraft and covered islands Japan controls. Zones usually avoid disputed territory and do not overlap. Japan warned of unpredictable events and the United States objected. South Korea then expanded its own zone so that it partly overlapped those of China and Japan. China's zone is still declared.

For anyone thinking of a floating or flying settlement, the point is practical. Open-ocean sky is not owned by any country, yet a platform there may still find a nearby government asking it to report, and sending fighters to look when it does not. Such a zone gives the declaring country no ownership of the air. It shows how far a country can reach in practice without any new law.
adiz-high-seas.mechanism: A state can extend practical control over the air above the open ocean by imposing reporting rules, without claiming to own that air. Whether this is lawful remains disputed, and it continues because other states have mostly tolerated it.

tokyo-convention-aircraft-flag.story:
The Tokyo Convention is a treaty signed in Tokyo on 14 September 1963 that settles which country's law applies to crimes on board an aircraft in flight. Before such rules, a crime over the open ocean, or over a place no country rules, could leave no one clearly responsible. The treaty fills that gap. It does not cover state aircraft used for military, customs or police work.

The answer it gives is the state of registration, the country on whose list the aircraft is entered. Article 3 says that country has power over crimes committed on board, and each party must make sure its own law provides for this. The arrangement resembles the rule for ships, which fall under the law of the country whose flag they fly. A Panama-registered aircraft over Antarctica therefore carries Panamanian criminal law inside it, and passengers cannot claim they have left all legal systems behind.

Other countries' power is limited. Article 4 allows a party that is not the country of registration to interfere with a plane in flight, to enforce its criminal law, only in a few exceptional situations. A law review article from India describes jurisdiction, meaning legal authority, as resting first with the country of registration, with other countries sharing some powers.

The treaty also deals with what happens in the cabin, since police are not on hand. The commander, the crew and in some cases passengers may act to prevent offences. The commander may restrain someone, put an offender off the plane at a landing or hand them to the authorities there.

Suppose a group built a large aircraft or airship to live on outside every country. If it is registered, the law of the registering country follows it, including over open ocean. If it refuses registration, the Chicago Convention's rules on nationality and airworthiness are not met, and other countries have reason to bar it from their airspace and airports. Registering in a small country with light rules moves the question without removing it, since the aircraft is still under one country's power.

add_sources.t: Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation, Wikipedia

tokyo-convention-aircraft-flag.mechanism: Registering an aircraft attaches one country's law to it, even over places no state owns. An aircraft cannot escape national law simply by flying somewhere outside every country.

chicago-convention.story:
The Chicago Convention is the main treaty on international civil aviation. Near the end of the Second World War, governments knew that long-distance flying would soon be routine, and they wanted common rules on who may fly where. Fifty-two states signed in Chicago on 7 December 1944. It came into force on 4 April 1947, the same day the International Civil Aviation Organization, the United Nations aviation agency, began work. It now has 193 parties, including every United Nations member except Liechtenstein.

Article 1 is the rule that matters most here. Every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty, meaning supreme legal authority, over the airspace above its territory. Article 2 defines territory as a state's land and the territorial waters next to it, the coastal belt it fully controls. This continues a rule from the 1919 Paris Convention, and scholars trace both to an old Roman-law saying that whoever owns the soil owns up to the sky. A foreign aircraft has no general right to be there. Scheduled airlines need permission.

The treaty also settles what an aircraft is in law. Under Articles 17 and 18 an aircraft has the nationality of the state in which it is registered and cannot be validly registered in more than one. Article 3 limits the treaty to civil aircraft, leaving out military, customs and police aircraft. Over the open ocean beyond the coastal belt, Article 12 says the rules are those set under the Convention, so the air there is regulated even though no country owns it. A 2023 commentary on the Chinese balloon shot down by the United States noted that a balloon also counts as an aircraft under this treaty.

The treaty never says how high a state's sovereignty goes, and no later agreement has settled the height. Balloon flights, space planes and proposals for floating cities therefore keep raising the same question.

For someone hoping to found a place in the sky, this treaty closes most routes. Anything above land or territorial waters is already in a country's air and needs that country's consent. Anything above open ocean still needs a nationality and must follow the rules of the air. A platform with no registration would have no treaty right to enter anyone's airspace or land at anyone's airport.

add_sources.t: Shooting down Chinese high-altitude balloon: Unlawful use of force?, Leiden Law Blog, 13 Mar 2023

chicago-convention.mechanism: Airspace is treated as part of a country's territory. The air above a state's land or territorial waters already belongs to that state, so no new country can be set up there without its consent, and aircraft elsewhere carry the nationality of the country that registers them.

us-v-causby.story:
United States v. Causby is a 1946 decision of the American Supreme Court on whether a landowner owns the sky above their land. It decided that a person does not, while also protecting the air close to the ground. It is on the map because it answers a tempting idea, that someone could buy a plot and claim a private domain straight up above it.

The Causby family owned 2.8 acres near an airport outside Greensboro, North Carolina, with a house and outbuildings used mainly for raising chickens. The end of a runway lay 2,220 feet from their barn. From May 1942 the American military used the airport, and bombers, transports and fighters passed over the property on their glide path, as low as 83 feet, which was 67 feet above the house and 18 feet above the highest tree. The Court recorded that planes blew old leaves off the trees and that the noise was startling. Terrified chickens flew into the walls and about 150 died, so the family gave up the chicken business. They also lost sleep.

The family argued that the government had taken their property. The Fifth Amendment to the Constitution requires payment when it does so. A lower court, the Court of Claims, agreed and valued the loss at $2,000. The government answered that Congress had declared national sovereignty over the air, with a public right of transit through navigable airspace, so there was no taking at all.

The old common-law rule, written in Latin as cujus est solum ejus est usque ad coelum, says that whoever owns the soil owns everything up to the sky. Justice Douglas, writing for the Court, said that this doctrine has no place in the modern world and that the air is a public highway. If the rule stood, every transcontinental flight would expose its operator to countless trespass suits. So the sky above the land belongs to no private owner. The owner does hold at least as much space as can be occupied or used in connection with the land, because otherwise nobody could put up a building or plant a tree. Flights count as a taking only if they are so low and so frequent as to interfere directly and immediately with the use of the land. Airspace above that level is public, and the Court declined to set the exact height.

The family therefore won on the principle, and the case went back to the lower court because its findings did not describe what had been taken. Justice Black dissented.

For anyone hoping to claim the air above a plot of land, the ruling limits the claim to the low air needed to use that land. Above it, the air is under the national government's control and open to traffic. A later owner gains no separate territory by building upward.
us-v-causby.mechanism: Ownership of land does not extend indefinitely upward. A landowner has rights only in the low air needed to use the land, and so cannot found a private domain in the sky above it.
us-v-causby.why: Added the outcome. The Supreme Court reversed the judgment and sent the case back for findings on what had been taken, so the family did not end with a final award from this decision.

antarctic-claims-article-iv.story:
Antarctica is a continent of ice with no native human population, and seven countries claim parts of it, in eight separate claims. A treaty has frozen those claims since 1961. Understanding why matters to anyone who looks at the map, sees empty land and wonders whether they could claim some of it.

The claims grew mainly out of whaling and rivalry. France dates its claim to Adélie Land from 1840, when the explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville landed there and named it after his wife. Britain's dates from 1908, when it said it needed to regulate and tax whaling, and in 1917 it extended the claim toward the South Pole. In 1923 Britain created the Ross Dependency under New Zealand's governor, and in 1933 it transferred a huge sector to Australia. Norway claimed Peter I Island in 1931 and Queen Maud Land in 1939 to protect its whalers, Chile claimed a sector in 1940 and Argentina in the 1940s. Argentina and Chile also point to old Spanish grants. Most claims are slices meeting at the pole. Those of Argentina, Chile and Britain overlap, and in 1943 Britain began Operation Tabarin to put people on the ground and support its position.

The countries that made no claim saw the matter differently. In the International Geophysical Year of 1957 and 1958, a large scientific effort, 12 countries worked there. They signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington on 1 December 1959, and it came into force on 23 June 1961. It now has 58 parties. It keeps the continent for peaceful use and science and bans military activity.

Article IV settles the dispute by pausing it. No side has to give up its position or accept anyone else's. Nothing done while the treaty is in force can support or deny a claim or create rights of sovereignty, meaning legal ownership by a state, and no new claim or enlargement can be made. A country can therefore run a station, register a birth or plant a flag without changing the legal position by a single metre. That removes the reason to race for land.

The results are unusual. Other countries do not recognise the claims, and the United States and Russia keep the right to make claims of their own. Countries without claims, such as China and India, run research stations on land others claim. Marie Byrd Land, about 1.6 million square kilometres, remains unclaimed, though Article IV bars anyone from claiming it now. A 1991 agreement, the Madrid Protocol, added a ban on mining.

So a private person cannot acquire any of it. A new claim has no effect.
antarctic-claims-article-iv.mechanism: A treaty can freeze a dispute over territory. Under Article IV all sides keep their positions, nothing done during the freeze counts for or against them, and new claims are barred, including on land nobody has claimed.

esperanza-base-births.story:
Esperanza Base is an Argentine research station at Hope Bay, near the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula, the long arm of the continent that reaches toward South America. It has 43 buildings, and in winter it houses 56 people, including 10 families and 2 teachers. Argentina, Chile and Britain all claim this land, and Argentina has spent decades showing that it governs here.

The spot has a history of friction. In 1952 an Argentine shore party fired a machine gun over the heads of a British team unloading supplies to rebuild its base, reportedly the only shots fired in anger on the continent. Argentina apologised, saying a commander had exceeded his authority, and the British finished rebuilding with a military escort. Argentina built its base in 1953.

Families and babies served a legal purpose here. Under ordinary international law, a country strengthens a claim by showing that it actually runs a place, with officials, registers and schools. In late 1977 Silvia Morella de Palma, seven months pregnant and the wife of the army detachment's commander, Captain Jorge Palma, was flown in. Her son Emilio was born on 7 January 1978, weighing 3.4 kilograms, and was baptised at the base chapel. Most sources treat him as the first person born on the Antarctic mainland. ExplorersWeb describes the flight as part of an Argentine initiative to strengthen its territorial presence. A school opened in 1978, a radio station began in 1979, and an Argentine civil register office records births and weddings. About 1,100 tourists visit each year.

Marisa Delgado was born there in May of the same year. Some sources count 11 births in Antarctica, eight at Esperanza and three at Chile's Frei base.

Palma's citizenship shows the tangle. He is Argentine through his parents, and because he was born before 1983 on land Britain claims, he is also reported to have had British citizenship. There is no Antarctic nationality and no Antarctic passport. A child born there simply takes whatever passport a parent's country gives.

The legal value of all this is close to nothing. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty, which came into force in 1961, says acts done while the treaty lasts cannot support a claim. So the births and registers remain as facts on the ground, with effect only if the treaty someday ends.
esperanza-base-births.mechanism: Births and civil registers are classic evidence that a state governs a piece of land. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty says acts done while the treaty is in force cannot support a claim, so they add nothing to Argentina's.

villa-las-estrellas.story:
Villa Las Estrellas is a small Chilean settlement for civilians and military families on King George Island, in the South Shetland Islands off the Antarctic Peninsula. It is attached to the Eduardo Frei air base. A gravel runway is the main way in and out, used by military transport planes from the far south of Chile. Chile treats the settlement as part of the commune of Antartica in its Magallanes region, while Argentina and Britain also claim the land.

Families moved in on 15 February 1984 and the village was formally founded that April, with a school opening the same day. It later gained a civil registry, post office, bank, library and church, and 14 family homes stand there. Most people are scientists and air force or navy staff on rotation, and those on long postings often bring spouses and children. BBC Future gave a figure of about 100 people when it visited in 2018, and other counts give about 150 in summer and 80 in winter, with 41 in a 2013 count of the civilian settlement.

The base commander told the BBC he had spent more than two years there with his wife and son, and that a winter at minus 47 degrees had kept them indoors for weeks. Long-stay residents, children included, have their appendix removed before coming, because the nearest major hospital is more than 1,000 kilometres away across the Southern Ocean and the few doctors on base are not specialist surgeons. Pregnancy is discouraged.

The settlement was also part of how Chile showed that it governed the area. Juan Pablo Camacho, born there in November 1984, was the first Chilean born in Antarctic territory, and at a ceremony in the presidential palace the country's ruler Augusto Pinochet gave him life insurance and funding for his studies. The local radio station is named Radio Soberania, meaning sovereignty.

Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty says nothing done there while the treaty lasts can strengthen a claim. The village shows what a settlement in Antarctica takes in practice, with military flights, a state school and an air base alongside it. The village remains inhabited today, with people on rotating postings.
villa-las-estrellas.mechanism: Families, a school and a civil registry are normal evidence that a state governs a place. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty says they cannot add to Chile's legal claim while the treaty lasts.

world-park-base.story:
World Park Base was a year-round camp that the environmental group Greenpeace ran at Cape Evans on Ross Island, Antarctica, from 1987 to 1992. It stood in the part of the continent New Zealand claims, and it remains the only non-government year-round base there has been. Nobody there claimed the land or declared a state. It is on the map because a private group used a physical presence to gain influence in the one continent run entirely by governments.

The background is how Antarctica is governed. Countries that do substantial research there meet under the Antarctic Treaty and make decisions by consensus. Between 1982 and 1988 these countries negotiated a treaty, the Convention on the Regulation of Antarctic Mineral Resource Activities, that would have set rules for mining if it ever came. Supporters called it a precaution. Greenpeace wanted the opposite outcome, a protected World Park off-limits to commercial use, with only limited science. It built a base to earn a voice at treaty meetings and to find allies. Having a year-round station was the normal way a country showed that it was serious about Antarctica.

The treaty governments officially ignored the base and gave it no help, though New Zealand would have helped in a life-threatening emergency. A private operator in that position could not count on government help for anything short of a life-threatening emergency.

A British Antarctic Survey account says Greenpeace and other groups challenged the treaty countries with unprecedented public scrutiny in the 1980s. Australia and France withdrew their support for the mining treaty, and it failed to gain enough support by its deadline of 25 November 1989. A new agreement, the Protocol on Environmental Protection, was signed in Madrid in 1991 and came into force in 1998. It designates Antarctica as a natural reserve devoted to peace and science.

With that aim met, Greenpeace closed the base in 1991 and removed it in 1991 and 1992. A study in the journal Polar Record estimated total fuel spills at under 200 litres, with contamination in one spot reaching 70 centimetres into the frozen ground. The case shows that a private group can occupy a site and shape policy from it, and that this gave it no land and no legal status. It also left when its goal was reached.
world-park-base.mechanism: A private group gained political influence in Antarctica by occupying a site and campaigning from it, without claiming any land or asking for any legal status.

flandrensis.story:
The Grand Duchy of Flandrensis is a self-declared country with no people on its land, a kind of hobby state called a micronation. It claims five islands off West Antarctica: Siple, Cherry, Maher, Pranke and Carney. Niels Vermeersch of Belgium started it on 4 September 2008 as a two-week hobby, drawing on the medieval County of Flanders.

It grew into something closer to a club with state furniture. It had identity cards, a currency, a newspaper, a constitution, an anthem and a football team, and until 2014 it ran partly as a political simulation with parties and yearly elections. The islands lie off the part of West Antarctica that no country has claimed. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty bars new claims, so the claim has no legal effect, and nobody has had reason to test it.

It has since described itself as an ecological project to draw attention to melting ice. In 2021 it registered in Belgium as a non-profit, which gave it a real legal form under Belgian law, and counted 741 citizens of 71 nationalities. It says it does not seek diplomatic recognition, meaning acceptance by real governments, and does not intend to visit its islands. Its founder spoke at the ChangeNOW climate summit in Paris in 2022, and the project co-hosted the first European MicroCon, a micronation meeting, at Ypres in August 2023. That is its most recent reported activity.
flandrensis.mechanism: A claim to land no one can live on can serve as publicity for conservation, with no attempt to gain legal ownership. The only legal status it holds is as a non-profit in an existing country.

talossa-antarctic-claim.story:
The Kingdom of Talossa is a self-declared country, or micronation, that began as a teenager's project in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and that also claims a part of Antarctica. Robert Ben Madison, aged 14, founded it in his bedroom on 26 December 1979, shortly after his mother died. He took the name after finding that it means inside the house in Finnish. Through his teens he produced a handwritten newspaper, a flag and an emblem, with about a dozen relatives and friends as members.

In 1980 he began inventing a Talossan language, mostly French-based, which now claims 35,000 root words and has its own language committee. Talossa is known for the language and for its internet presence, and it has never run a territory. It has had a website since 1995. Stories in the New York Times and Wired in the mid-1990s brought in new citizens, and that web presence helped inspire later internet micronations. Madison ended his kingdom in late 2005, but Talossa kept going without him. He registered the name as a service mark and created a non-profit corporation in Wisconsin, and by 2013 the mark had been cancelled and the corporation dissolved.

Its claim covers the east side of Milwaukee, the small French island of Cezembre and part of Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica, the area no country claims. Its members live elsewhere and none on the Antarctic land. In 2000 Wired described it as one of the projects that claim territory but would not take power if offered it. Milwaukee remains under American law and Cezembre under French law. Marie Byrd Land is closed to new claims by the Antarctic Treaty.

On 5 August 2023 it counted 157 active citizens and 564 registered people in all. No state or United Nations body recognises any of the territory claimed.
talossa-antarctic-claim.mechanism: The Antarctic Treaty bars new claims on the continent, so a hobby state's claim there has no legal effect. Nobody has needed to inspect or contest it either.

westarctica.story:
The Grand Duchy of Westarctica is a self-declared country, or micronation, claiming Marie Byrd Land, about 1.6 million square kilometres of West Antarctica and the one large area no country claims. In 2001 Travis McHenry, a United States Navy intelligence specialist, read in the CIA World Factbook that no state had claimed it, and he declared the Protectorate of Westarctica. He wrote letters to many countries over the years, but only other micronations responded with recognition.

Having no land to run, the project lived on paper and online, with a flag, a coat of arms, a currency called the Ice Mark and titles of nobility. In 2004 McHenry began issuing fantasy passports as souvenirs, and he stopped after learning that a scammer in Kenya was selling them to refugees as real travel documents. By 2006 his Navy superiors knew he was writing to foreign governments and told him to choose. He kept his job and gave the title of Grand Duke to a friend, Philip Karns. After leaving the Navy he started another micronation, Calsahara, in the Californian desert, which was merged into Westarctica, and he took back the title in 2010.

In 2014 he registered Westarctica in Sacramento as a non-profit under American tax law, and it now campaigns on climate change and offers a research scholarship. It reports over 5,000 members as of 2018 and hosted a micronation meeting, MicroCon, in Las Vegas in 2022. It says a Russian polar research institute gave it permission to use an abandoned research station during a planned trip.

The risk of official-looking papers came up again. In July 2025 Indian police arrested Harsh Vardhan Jain for running a fake Westarctica embassy from a rented house in Ghaziabad, with false diplomatic number plates, fake passports and stamps, and money linked to suspected laundering. Westarctica acknowledged that he had served as its Consul-General to India while disowning the plates and documents.

Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty forbids any new claim while the treaty is in force, so the claim has no legal standing, even over land no country has claimed. McHenry found a real gap on the map, and the treaty had closed it decades before he arrived. Westarctica continues as an online project with no one on the land.
westarctica.mechanism: Even the one large unclaimed part of Antarctica cannot be claimed, because the Antarctic Treaty bars new claims. Documents issued for a private claim can still be misused by others as if they were real.

chernobyl-samosely.story:
The samosely, meaning self-settlers, are people who live inside the 30-kilometre Chernobyl Exclusion Zone in Ukraine and Belarus without official approval. The zone is the area around the nuclear plant emptied after the 1986 disaster, when about 100,000 people were evacuated. It holds abandoned towns and villages, and living there is still prohibited. Some people refused to leave and others slipped back after the area was sealed off.

Their reasons were mostly personal. About 1,200 people returned in 1986. Most were elderly people who had lived there before the disaster. Many had been told they could go home in a few days, and they then faced discrimination in the areas where they were resettled. A few outsiders came as well, escaping poverty or, after 2014, the war in Donbas. They live scattered through the city of Chernobyl and about 11 villages, some with only a handful of people.

Their legal position is unusual and has never amounted to independence. Ukraine has not legalised their settlements. Local officials in 2012 unofficially let elderly people stay while ordering younger ones out, and in April 2013 the social policy minister said the settlers receive full social support but that legalisation was impossible because living in the zone is forbidden. So the state that bans their presence also supports them. It treats them as its citizens who are breaking a rule, and it does not treat them as a separate community.

There has been almost no next generation. In the first 25 years the zone recorded more than 900 deaths and one known birth, a girl born in 1999 who later went to boarding school outside it. Numbers have fallen mainly through old age, from 314 in a 2007 census to 135 in 2017. Russian forces occupied the area in 2022, and residents have described that time as frightening. A Ukrainian report in April 2026 put the number left at about 25.

None of them has declared a separate state. The zone shows that an abandoned place with weak policing is not a place without a government, and that people who stay there depend on the same state they are defying.
chernobyl-samosely.mechanism: A government's evacuation order may go unenforced in practice, but people who stay gain no separate legal standing and remain under that government's law, often relying on its pensions and services.

cyprus-buffer-zone-pyla.story:
The United Nations Buffer Zone, also called the Green Line, is a strip of land patrolled by peacekeepers that runs 180 kilometres across the Mediterranean island of Cyprus. It covers 346 square kilometres and ranges from under 20 metres to over 7 kilometres wide, and it cuts through the centre of the capital, Nicosia. Looked at on a map, it seems to be land between two countries, which is why it belongs in a study of places outside every country.

It began with a pencil line. After fighting between Greek and Turkish Cypriots at Christmas 1963, a British general, Peter Young, drew an agreed ceasefire line on a map with a green chinagraph pencil on 30 December 1963. The United Nations force took over in 1964. In July 1974, after a short-lived Greek Cypriot coup, Turkey invaded and took about 37 per cent of the island. A ceasefire followed on 16 August, and the Security Council backed a security zone that only United Nations forces could enter. Today the zone marks the limit of the Turkish advance. North of it is the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is largely unrecognised, and south of it is the Republic of Cyprus.

The strip is not empty. About 10,000 people live and farm in villages inside it, including Deneia, Athienou and Troulloi. Pyla is known as one of the few villages left in Cyprus where Greek and Turkish Cypriots live side by side. Elsewhere, untouched areas have become refuges for plants and animals, and the Turkish army has built fences, walls, watchtowers and minefields on its northern side. Crossing was very limited until 2003, when the rules were relaxed after nearly 30 years. In March 2021 Cyprus put up a barbed wire fence on part of the zone.

In law the strip is not a territory of its own. The United Nations patrols it under a ceasefire and does not own or rule it as a state, and the claims of the governments on either side continue. Residents remain tied to one of those communities. No one has been reported trying to declare a separate state there, and it remains under United Nations patrol.
cyprus-buffer-zone-pyla.mechanism: A strip of land patrolled by peacekeepers does not end the claims of the states on either side, so people living inside it stay part of an existing state.

korean-dmz-villages.story:
The Korean Demilitarized Zone is a strip about 250 kilometres long and 4 kilometres wide separating North and South Korea. It was created by the armistice, or ceasefire agreement, of 27 July 1953, when each side moved its troops back 2,000 metres from the front line. No peace treaty followed, so the zone is still managed under that ceasefire. Its edges are among the most heavily armed borders in the world. Two villages are allowed to remain inside it, by decision of the armistice committee.

Daeseong-dong, also called Tae Sung Dong or Freedom Village, is on the southern side and is governed and protected by the United Nations Command. Its residents, 218 people in 2008, descend from those who owned the land before the war. They must generally spend at least 240 nights a year there to keep their residency. They count as South Korean citizens but do not pay tax or do military service. In the 1980s South Korea put up a 100-metre flagpole there.

Kijŏng-dong, or Peace Village, is on the northern side, about 1.2 kilometres from the line, with brightly painted concrete buildings that were meant to be visible across the border. Observers using telescopic lenses have reported that the buildings are shells without window glass or interior rooms. North Korea answered the southern flagpole with a 160-metre one. Only North Korea or the United Nations Command can give access to the zone.

In other words these are not free spaces between two countries. Every aspect of daily life depends on the military bodies that run the ceasefire, and residents keep the citizenship of one side. Both villages remain in place under the armistice.
korean-dmz-villages.mechanism: Living inside an armistice zone depends on permission from the bodies that run the ceasefire, and residents keep the citizenship of a country on one side.

luxembourg-space-resources-2017.story:
This is a law Luxembourg passed on 20 July 2017 saying companies can own materials they mine in space, the first such law in Europe. Luxembourg is a small European country, and in 2016 it announced a programme called SpaceResources.lu to attract space mining firms. At the time only the United States had a similar law.

Article 1 says that space resources are capable of being owned. The rest sets out how a company gets government approval for a mission and how officials supervise it. The procedures were largely modelled on those used for the financial sector. So a company would apply for a licence, much as a bank or fund does there, and then operate under supervision.

Luxembourg set out to be more open than the United States in two ways. The American law protects only United States citizens, while Luxembourg's is not tied to nationality, so a foreign-owned company with a Luxembourg base can use it. Export controls on space technology are also seen as lighter in Europe, which the law firm commentary treats as a selling point for firms that find American rules on selling hardware and hiring foreigners burdensome.

The difficulty is Article II of the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main international agreement on space, which binds Luxembourg and 104 other countries. It says outer space, including the Moon and other bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by use or occupation, or by any other means. The treaty does not directly mention private owners or mined materials. Scholars are split on whether a country may give private property rights in what is extracted. Luxembourg's own Council of State, which advises on new laws, said it was unclear whether international law allows this. The law tries to avoid the conflict by covering only the materials and saying nothing about ownership of the Moon or an asteroid. Think of a fishing licence, which covers the fish caught and not the sea.

For someone hoping to found a place in space, this law gives very little. It offers rights to what a mission brings out of the ground, and a government supervisor. It offers no land and no right to rule anything. Other countries are not bound to respect the title, since only international agreement could make them do so, and the commentary itself says domestic law will need to be complemented by international accords.

The two best-known asteroid mining firms of that period, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, were both sold by January 2019. No court has tested the law.
luxembourg-space-resources-2017.mechanism: A small country can offer space miners a legal home by licensing them, and companies can then choose whichever country's law suits them best. The law covers mined materials and avoids any claim to land in space.

nemitz-eros.story:
Eros is an asteroid, a large rock orbiting the Sun. Gregory Nemitz, an aerospace consultant from Carson City, Nevada, published a claim of ownership over it in March 2000, under the name of the Eros Project for Space Property Law. He had never been there and had no plan to go. His purpose was to force a court to say whether private people can own property in space. His view, in his own words, was that there will be no commercial activities in space without official respect for private property rights.

His chance came on 12 February 2001, when NASA, the American space agency, landed its NEAR Shoemaker probe on Eros and left it there. Nemitz sent NASA an invoice for $20, the parking and storage fee for the next century. The amount was nominal. An unpaid bill gave him something he could take to court.

NASA refused to pay, with its lawyer saying the claim appeared to have no foundation in law. Nemitz then wrote to the State Department, which replied that in its view private ownership of an asteroid is precluded by Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space. That article says that outer space and bodies in it are not subject to national appropriation by claim, use, occupation or any other means. Its words speak of national appropriation, which left open the question Nemitz wanted answered, whether a private owner is covered too.

On 3 November 2003 he filed a complaint in federal court in Reno asking for a declaratory judgment, a ruling that states what the law is without ordering payment. His question was whether the treaty rules out private ownership of asteroids or property on other bodies. The judge, Howard McKibben, ordered the case dismissed in April 2004. Nemitz appealed in July to the Ninth Circuit, a federal appeals court in San Francisco, citing a presidential commission that had just warned that uncertain property rights could strangle a space industry. The claim was dismissed in 2005.

Press and bloggers called this the first legal case on property in space. As a precedent it is thin, since it was dismissed and no reported ruling explains the treaty, and a writer at Reason observed that a claimant who has never been anywhere near the asteroid is easy to distinguish from a serious miner. Its main result was a written American government position against private ownership of an asteroid. Ten years later, in 2015, Congress took a different path by giving Americans ownership of what they mine, while disclaiming any ownership of the asteroid itself.
nemitz-eros.mechanism: The American State Department said Article II of the Outer Space Treaty rules out private ownership of an asteroid, and the courts refused to give Nemitz ownership. Announcing a claim without going there gave him nothing a court would act on.

planetary-resources-dsi.story:
Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries were two companies, announced in the early 2010s, that planned to mine asteroids. Their idea was to prospect asteroids and extract resources such as water ice, then find uses for them in space. They are on the map because their plans helped push governments to write laws on who owns what is mined in space.

Planetary Resources announced itself in 2012 with prominent business backers. Nine months later Deep Space Industries, founded by entrepreneurs and space advocates, announced similar plans. Both built small spacecraft, and both stood to gain when the United States in 2015 and Luxembourg in 2017 passed laws on who owns materials mined in space. A presidential commission had warned in 2004 that no company would invest in a product whose legal ownership was uncertain, and these laws addressed that worry even though no mine existed.

The business proved much harder than the law. An asteroid mining company needed the patience to develop technology for prospecting and extraction, and then needed customers in space for what it found. Those customers did not yet exist. Most spacecraft use fuels such as hydrazine that are not available from asteroids, so Deep Space Industries built a small engine called Comet that runs on water, partly to create future demand. Its work drifted toward small-satellite parts, where buyers already existed.

Their money ran out before any mining began. In 2017 a funding round for Planetary Resources with a major mining company fell through, which led to large layoffs. In October 2018 the blockchain firm ConsenSys bought it on undisclosed terms and named only two of its people as staying. On 1 January 2019 Bradford Space announced that it had bought Deep Space Industries, chiefly for its engine, its customers and its engineers. Jeff Foust, writing in The Space Review, concluded that the asteroid mining boom had been a bubble.

The laws they helped inspire remain in force after both firms were sold. For anyone planning a settlement in space, the case shows that a favourable law is the easy part compared with funding a mission that has no paying customer at the far end.

planetary-resources-dsi.mechanism: National laws on owning materials mined in space were written with these firms in mind, and those laws remain in force after the firms were sold. They came before any actual mining took place.

uae-japan-space-resources.story:
These are laws from the United Arab Emirates and Japan that allow companies to use materials mined in space, following the United States in 2015 and Luxembourg in 2017. The Emirates was also working with a private Japanese company on a Moon landing planned for 2022.

The Emirates' Federal Law No. 12 of 2019 is a general space law. It covers licensing, registering spacecraft, liability and insurance, along with rules on building facilities on other planets and on using space resources. It had come into force by early 2020. Japan's parliament, the Diet, then passed Act No. 83 of 2021, on business activities in exploring and developing space resources, which made Japan the fourth country to pass such a law. Article 5 is headed Acquisition of Ownership of Space Resources. According to the news site Atalayar the law lets Japanese companies find, extract and own minerals from the surface and subsurface of the Moon, Mars or other bodies, under the umbrella of Japan's international space agreements. Japan's Hayabusa 2 mission had returned a few grams of dust from the asteroid Ryugu in December 2020, which showed that extraction is possible on a small scale.

The legal idea is that national practice can gradually shape international law. Treaties are one source of international law, and another is custom, the consistent practice of states that they treat as lawful. When several countries pass similar laws and others do not object, this can start to count as custom. Together with the American and Luxembourg laws, these acts form a growing group of countries treating mining as a lawful use of space. A rule formed in this way has not yet been established.

No international treaty authorises this. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty still bars any country from claiming a body in space, and these laws give ownership of materials and not of ground. A person living at a mine on the Moon under these laws would remain under the licensing country's supervision. No court has tested the laws.
uae-japan-space-resources.mechanism: When several countries pass similar laws, their shared practice can start to shape international law. These countries are building that practice for ownership of mined space materials without any treaty authorising it.

us-space-act-2015.story:
This is an American law, signed on 25 November 2015, that gives American companies ownership of materials they mine in space. It is Title IV of the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, and its main rule became Section 51303 of Title 51 of the United States Code. A presidential commission had warned in 2004 that uncertainty over who owns space materials could strangle a space industry at the start, since no company would invest in a product it might not legally own.

The rule is short. A United States citizen engaged in commercial recovery of an asteroid resource or a space resource is entitled to whatever is obtained, including to possess, own, transport, use and sell it, in accordance with applicable law, including the international obligations of the United States. It applies only to United States citizens, so a foreign firm gains nothing from it.

It had to be written carefully because of the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main international agreement on space. Article I says the use of space is the province of all mankind and must benefit all countries. Article II says that outer space and bodies in it are not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by use or occupation, or by any other means. Opinio Juris, a law blog, wrote that Congress avoided a conflict in three ways. The right goes to private citizens and not to the nation. It is subject to international obligations. And the Act states that the United States does not assert sovereignty, meaning national ownership, or exclusive rights over any body in space.

So a company could own a tonne of mined ore while nobody owned the asteroid. A familiar comparison is fishing on the high seas, where a boat owns what it catches although no one owns the ocean. The same Opinio Juris writer, who supported the law, pointed out that other countries could then do the same for their own citizens, leaving the matter to each country's rules. Critics argued that the law breaches the treaty.

Luxembourg copied the idea in 2017, and others followed. The law offers nothing to someone wanting territory. It grants no land, no settlement and no right to govern, and it expressly disclaims those things. Whether one country can grant rights that others must respect is still debated, and no court ruling on the question has been reported.

us-space-act-2015.mechanism: American law grants ownership of mined materials while disclaiming any national ownership of the asteroid or moon they came from. This set the model of rights to the resources without rights to the land.

assab-rubattino.story:
