Assab is a port in Eritrea on the Red Sea, near the Bab-el-Mandeb strait at the sea's southern end. In the middle of the 19th century it was an Afar fishing village of about 100 people. Its value lay in its position.

On 15 November 1869 an Italian missionary, Giuseppe Sapeto, bought the bay on behalf of the Rubattino Shipping Company from two brothers, the sultans Hasan and Ibrahim ibn Ahmed, for 6,000 Maria Theresa thalers, a silver coin widely used in the region. Sapeto argued that the port was well placed near the strait, and that it was nominally under the sultan of Aussa but really independent, which would mean the brothers had the right to sell.

Others did not agree. The press and parliament in Italy opposed the purchase, and Egypt declared the sale illegal. A company could hold the title, but it could not defend a claim against another government.

The Italian government, seeing a route inland to Ethiopia, took control of the port in 1882. Italian envoys then used it as a trade link. Count Pietro Antonelli agreed to supply Menelik II of Shewa with Remington rifles through Assab, and by the following year he had brought in 50,000 rifles in exchange for camels bearing gold, ivory and civet. A visitor in 1884 counted 111 Afars, 140 Arabs, 43 Italians, 12 Abyssinians and 10 Somalis. This foothold led to the colony of Italian Eritrea. A private purchase here became a state colony once the state decided to take it over.
assab-rubattino.mechanism: A company bought the land and the state later stepped in to hold it. Egypt's protest shows that a sale by local rulers does not settle who has the right to sell.

batmans-treaty.story:
Batman's Treaty was an 1835 attempt by British colonists to buy the land where Melbourne, Australia, now stands directly from its Aboriginal owners. It is considered the first and only documented time Europeans negotiated their presence directly with the traditional owners. To follow what happened, it helps to know the colonial rule. Britain treated all of Australia as Crown land. Settlers could get land only by grant from the government, and settlement was limited to certain approved districts. Port Phillip lay beyond them.

The Port Phillip Association was a group of sheep farmers based mostly in Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania), who wanted new pasture across the strait. John Batman and the lawyer Joseph Gellibrand had applied for a grant at Port Phillip in 1827 and been refused. In 1835 they tried another way. Gellibrand drew up a deed, a legal document transferring an interest in land, with a yearly tribute, and Batman sailed from Launceston on 10 May in a 23-ton schooner with seven Aboriginal men from New South Wales and a few others. They exchanged gifts with local people for about a week.

On 6 June he met eight Wurundjeri and Boonwurrung elders beside a stream, probably Merri Creek in what is now Northcote, though the place is disputed. For 600,000 acres he handed over 40 pairs of blankets, 42 tomahawks, 130 knives, 62 pairs of scissors, 40 looking glasses, 250 handkerchiefs, 18 shirts, 4 flannel jackets, 4 suits of clothes and 150 pounds of flour. Two days later Batman wrote in his journal that a spot on the river would be the place for a village, a line later called Melbourne's founding charter.

The objection came quickly. On 26 August the Governor of New South Wales, Richard Bourke, proclaimed such agreements void against the rights of the Crown and declared anyone on Crown land without authority a trespasser. The Colonial Office in London approved this in October. It objected that Batman had bought from Aboriginal people, whom British colonists did not accept had any claim to land, and that he had bought for the Association instead of the Crown.

The legal point has lasted. If the Aboriginal owners could sell, the Crown's claim to all land would be in question. So the proclamation denied their title and the buyer's together. A purchase from the people on the ground counted for nothing, because the only government with police and courts did not accept it.
batmans-treaty.mechanism: The Crown treated all land as its own, so a private purchase from the Aboriginal owners had no legal force. The governor cancelled the deal by proclamation.

benetton-patagonia.story:
The Italian clothing group Benetton is the largest private landowner in Argentina, holding about 970,000 hectares in Patagonia, the far south of the country, as ranch land. It bought the land in 1991 when it purchased the Compañía de Tierras Sud Argentino. That company dates from 1889, when the Argentine government gave land to 10 British citizens, 90,000 hectares each. The grant passed over the Mapuche people who lived there, many of whom ended up as labourers on the new ranches.

The case is on the map because it shows what buying land from a government does and does not buy. Benetton got ownership, and it has no government of its own there. Argentina's police and courts decide disputes, and those courts have treated the company's papers as decisive.

In 2002 a Mapuche couple, Atilio Curiñanco and Rosa Nahuelquir, moved with their children onto Santa Rosa, a 534-hectare part of the Leleque ranch, believing it was government land. The company complained, and police removed them and destroyed their home and crops. A judge cleared them of criminal blame, but ruled in the civil case that the land was Benetton's. In 2004 they travelled to Rome with the Nobel Peace laureate Adolfo Pérez Esquivel to meet Luciano Benetton, who promised to look for a solution.

He offered the Chubut provincial government 7,500 hectares elsewhere for Mapuche farming, and the province rejected it as unproductive. In February 2007, 25 Mapuche including six families occupied Santa Rosa again, saying it was their ancestral territory. In March 2011 Judge Omar Magallanes ruled for Benetton, gave the company the disputed land and ordered the residents to leave within 10 days. The community appealed, and how that appeal ended is not known.
benetton-patagonia.mechanism: The purchase gave the company legal ownership under Argentine law, and that ownership traces to an 1889 state grant made without the consent of the Mapuche. Argentina kept the right to rule the land, and its courts have treated the company's ownership as valid.

bolivian-syndicate-acre.story:
Acre is a region of rainforest in the western Amazon, now a state of Brazil. Around 1900 it mattered because of rubber, which was in high demand. Bolivia claimed it, but Brazilian rubber tappers were pouring in from the northeast of Brazil, and Bolivia's hold was weak.

Bolivia's answer was to lease the region out. The Bolivian Syndicate was an American and British investment company, set up through a firm in Jersey City, New Jersey. On 11 June 1901 Bolivia, under General José Manuel Pando, signed a 30-year lease that gave it almost total control of Acre, to occupy and exploit it. Bolivia hoped the arrangement would protect its hold. The company's shareholders are reported to have included the king of Belgium and relatives of President William McKinley of the United States.

Brazil and Peru claimed the territory too and objected strongly. Brazil saw a foreign company with powers close to a government's appearing on its frontier. It withdrew its consul and closed the Amazon's tributaries to Bolivian trade. Foreign powers protested because they regarded the river basin as international waters, and Brazil partly eased the ban.

On the ground, the rubber tappers acted first. In 1902 they hired a young Brazilian veteran, José Plácido de Castro, who on 6 August led 33 riflemen in canoes to capture the Bolivian depot at Xapuri. After setbacks he raised about a thousand men, sold thirty tons of rubber on a captured river boat to buy arms, and took the port of Puerto Alonso in January 1903. A short-lived Republic of Acre was declared, and Brazil's government sent troops.

Before major fighting between the two armies, the Brazilian diplomat Baron of Rio Branco negotiated a settlement. Under the Treaty of Petrópolis of November 1903 Bolivia gave Acre to Brazil in return for land in Mato Grosso, £2 million and a promised railway. The Syndicate was paid £110,000 to give up its lease.
bolivian-syndicate-acre.mechanism: A state tried to hold a remote region by leasing it to foreign investors with powers close to a government's. Neighbouring states refused to accept this, and the company was bought out when the region passed to Brazil by treaty.

british-north-borneo-company.story:
The British North Borneo Company was a private company that ran what is now Sabah, a state of Malaysia on the island of Borneo, for over 60 years. It is one of the clearest cases of a business becoming a government. It began with a deal made by Baron von Overbeck, a German businessman and diplomat, and the brothers Alfred and Edward Dent, who headed a British trading firm in Shanghai and London. They wanted a colonial concession, meaning a grant of rights over the land.

On 29 December 1877 the Sultan of Brunei agreed to one for 15,000 Spanish dollars. It then emerged that Brunei had already given some of the area to the Sultan of Sulu, so a second agreement was signed with him on 22 January 1878 for 5,000 dollars a year, with help from a Scottish adventurer named William Cowie. Overbeck and the Dents thereby became rulers of the territory on paper. Overbeck left in 1879 after failing to interest Germany. Alfred Dent turned to Britain, set up a provisional company with £300,000 of capital, and on 1 November 1881 received a royal charter, its legal authority to operate.

The charter is what changed the deal from private paper into something other governments would respect. The company then did what a state does. It recruited Sikh policemen from northern India, set up courts and prisons, levied taxes and built a railway from Jesselton to Tenom. Its governor sat at Sandakan, with districts run by officers and even named after directors, such as Dent and Alcock. Its first settlement, on Gaya Island, was burnt in a raid by a local leader, Mat Salleh, and resistance to its taxes continued for years. After Cowie joined the board in 1894, the company was run largely from London with shareholder returns uppermost, and Dent resigned. Britain made the territory a protectorate in 1888, meaning Britain took charge of its foreign relations.

The Second World War ended it. The company could not pay for rebuilding, so on 26 June 1946 it handed North Borneo to the Colonial Office, the British government department for colonies, for £860,000 in cash. In 1949 an independent arbitrator, a person appointed to settle the dispute, awarded a further £1.4 million, which disappointed shareholders, and share prices fell by almost half. The territory joined Malaysia in 1963.

The argument over the first deal has outlasted the company. The Sulu paper has been read both as a sale and as a lease. Malaysia kept paying the yearly fee to the sultan's heirs until 2013. Heirs then sought billions through private arbitration in Europe, and Malaysia won a final ruling in France's top court on 6 November 2024.
british-north-borneo-company.mechanism: Two local rulers signed away rights over land to private men, and a charter from Britain then gave the company the backing to govern it. Whether the Sulu agreement was a sale or a lease is still disputed.

casado-chaco.story:
The Chaco is a dry forest and scrub region covering western Paraguay. In the late 19th century the Paraguayan state sold off public land there. The Carlos Casado company, set up in Rosario, Argentina, was the biggest buyer of this kind. It acquired over 7,800 square kilometres in 1886 and came to hold more than 5 million hectares. It wanted quebracho, a tree whose wood yields tannin, a substance used for tanning hides.

The company then built what the state had not. It founded the town of Puerto Casado in 1889 on the Paraguay River and laid a narrow-gauge railway about 150 kilometres west into the forest. The founder's son, José Casado, came to manage it in 1929 and lived there until 1945. For a long time this was in effect a company town, with the owner's house, factory, port and rail line at its centre.

Paraguay still held the right to rule it. Mennonite settlers passed through from 1926 on company trains on their way to new colonies. When the Chaco War with Bolivia began, the port served as a military post, the commanding general lived in a house lent by the company, and the railway carried soldiers, supplies and wounded. Its workshops repaired the army's machinery.

The company stopped production in the late 1990s and its tannin factory is shut. It also sold its land, including the town, to a group called the Moon Sect, after the Korean religious leader Sun Myung Moon. Local residents, among them Guaraní people, marched nearly 600 kilometres to Asunción to ask the government to expropriate it, meaning take it over for public use.
casado-chaco.mechanism: A state sold public land to a company on a very large scale. The company owned the land and Paraguay kept the right to rule it, though the company's town and railway served the region.

cocos-clunies-ross.story:
The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are a small group of coral atolls in the Indian Ocean, now an Australian territory, that one Scottish family ran for about 150 years. The islands were empty until the 1820s. John Clunies-Ross, a Scottish merchant seaman, stopped there in 1825 and put up a British flag. When he returned in 1827 with his family, he found an Englishman, Alexander Hare, already settled there with a party of people of Malay origin, including about 40 women. A feud followed. Hare's people drifted away from him, and he left and died in 1834.

Clunies-Ross began harvesting coconuts. Labour came from the Malay Peninsula, the Indonesian islands, Southern Africa and New Guinea, as indentured workers, slaves or convicts, and much of today's population descends from them. They were paid in the Cocos rupee, a currency the family minted itself that could be redeemed only at the company store. The family owned the land, the store and the money.

Britain annexed the islands in 1857 and made the family head its Superintendent. In 1886 Queen Victoria granted all the land to the family in perpetuity. Sovereignty, the right to rule the islands, stayed with Britain, which ran them as part of its Singapore colony. In practice the head of the family served as resident magistrate, so the landlord and the local government were the same man. In 1955 the islands became a territory of Australia, and the family remained the landowner.

Australia's attitude changed in the 1970s. In 1978, under threat of compulsory purchase, the family sold its property for A$6.25 million, apart from their home, Oceania House, and its grounds on Home Island. In 1983 the government told John Cecil Clunies-Ross to leave. The High Court of Australia ruled in 1984 that taking Oceania House had been unlawful. The government then stopped using his shipping company, which contributed to his bankruptcy. On 6 April 1984 all 261 eligible islanders voted in a United Nations-supervised Act of Self Determination, with 229 for full integration with Australia, 21 for free association and nine for independence. Australia bought the last of his property in 1993 and sold Oceania House privately in 2001. A parliamentary report put the population at around 600, most of them Cocos Malays on Home Island.

The family's long hold ended within a few years of Australia deciding to buy it out.
cocos-clunies-ross.mechanism: The family legally owned all the land under a grant from the Crown, while Britain and then Australia kept the right to rule the islands. So the Australian government got control of the land by buying it, under threat of compulsory purchase.
cocos-clunies-ross.why: Added that the 1978 sale was made under threat of compulsory acquisition. The earlier wording suggested an ordinary purchase.

congo-free-state.story:
The Congo Free State was a state in Central Africa covering all of what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and it was the private possession of one man, King Leopold II of Belgium. It was not part of Belgium. The two countries only shared a monarch, an arrangement called a personal union. It is on the map as the largest case of a territory run as one person's private business.

Until the mid-19th century the Congo Basin was independent of Europe, because local resistance, rainforest and disease kept colonists out. Leopold wanted a colony. In 1876 he hosted a geographic conference in Brussels and set up a body presented as humanitarian. He then hired the explorer Henry Morton Stanley, who from 1879 to 1884 built roads and posts and signed treaties with local leaders that in effect gave Leopold rights over their land. One account from the time says the leaders who signed did not understand a word of them.

Treaties with local leaders were only paper until other governments accepted them. Leopold grouped them under a body called the International Association of the Congo. In April 1884 the United States became the first country to recognise the association's claim, after a lobbying campaign that used edited copies of the treaties. France followed, on condition that it got the first option to buy the territory if Leopold ever sold. The Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885, where European powers set rules for dividing Africa, then accepted the association under his personal control, after he promised humanitarian work and free trade. In 1885 he renamed it the Congo Free State.

He ran it from Brussels and never visited. He could not meet the costs of running it, so he looked for income. He declared vacant land, meaning any land without a house or garden plot, to be state property, which took in most of the country. A decree around 1890 said Africans in much of the state could sell ivory and rubber only to the state, at prices it set. From 1892 he granted huge concessions to private companies, which could police their areas as they saw fit, detain people and keep what the forest produced, paying him a share. Local rulers were paid in guns to collect rubber from their own people. Forced labour, torture and murder followed, and the highest estimates put deaths at half the population of the rubber provinces, though poor records make the number uncertain.

The British consul Roger Casement investigated and reported, and with the journalist E. D. Morel he founded the Congo Reform Association, which campaigned in Europe and America. Arthur Conan Doyle wrote a widely read book on the subject. Public and diplomatic pressure, along with Belgian investors who wanted the mining potential, led the Belgian Parliament reluctantly to annex the territory in 1908 as a colony called the Belgian Congo.

Recognition by outside powers turned a pile of treaties into a state, and the people living there were never asked to consent.
congo-free-state.mechanism: A private person turned bundles of treaties with local leaders into a state by persuading outside powers to recognise it, meaning to accept it as a state. Those powers later took away what they had granted when the abuses became a public scandal.

daewoo-madagascar.story:
In 2008 a South Korean company, Daewoo Logistics, agreed with the government of Madagascar to lease 1.3 million hectares of farmland for 99 years, an area larger than Qatar and by one report about half of the island's arable land. Madagascar is a large island off the east coast of Africa. Most of its people lived on less than a dollar a day, and nearly half of its children under five were malnourished, according to Mongabay.

The reason lay in world food prices. Prices had recently spiked, and South Korea, the world's third-largest buyer of corn, depended on imports mostly from the United States and South America. Daewoo aimed to replace over half of those imports. It would start with 2,000 hectares and eventually grow corn on 1 million hectares in the arid west and oil palm on 300,000 hectares in the east, the region holding most of the island's rainforest, all for export. It promised to spend $6 billion over 20 to 25 years on roads, railways, a port and schools. It was one of the largest of many such deals in Africa at the time.

A lease of this kind does not move a border, since Madagascar's law would still apply there. The deal mattered because the company would control land on the scale of a small country. Critics said it ignored local people's customary use of the land, the rights people hold through long use, and would take cropland in a country barely able to feed itself.

Anger over it helped fuel the movement against President Marc Ravalomanana, who had signed it, and he was driven from office on 17 March 2009. Andry Rajoelina, the 34-year-old mayor of the capital, replaced him and the next day said the deal was off. His reason was legal. The constitution, he said, stipulated that Madagascar's land was neither for sale nor for rent, and changing that would require consulting the people. He added that foreign investors were still welcome.

A few months later a campaign group, Rainforest Rescue, said Daewoo still held 218,000 hectares. How that claim was resolved is not known. The case shows that a land deal signed with one government can fall with that government, particularly when the people affected never agreed to it.
daewoo-madagascar.mechanism: A lease gives a company the use of land while the state keeps the right to rule it. The new leader cancelled this one on the ground that the constitution barred selling or renting out land.

de-thierry-hokianga.story:
Charles de Thierry, the son of a French family who had fled to England, tried to create his own sovereign state in New Zealand before the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840. At that time Britain had only a Resident, James Busby, on the scene, and the treaty that brought British rule had not yet been made.

While at Cambridge, de Thierry met Hongi Hika, a Ngāpuhi chief visiting England, and through the missionary Thomas Kendall arranged to buy 40,000 acres at Hokianga, a harbour in Northland, for 36 axes. After travels in North America and the Caribbean he reached the Pacific in 1835, announced himself King of Nuku Hiva in the Marquesas Islands, and wrote to Busby that he would land in New Zealand and set himself up as sovereign chief. He promised free trade, medicine and a share of benefits for local chiefs.

He recruited followers in Sydney in 1837 and sailed to Hokianga. There the chiefs Tāmati Wāka Nene and Patuone rejected his claims. They allowed him a plot of only 800 acres. His followers rioted and left, and he came to depend on Māori charity. He kept writing to France with inflated reports, pressing for a French colony under his own leadership.

The Treaty of Waitangi between the British Crown and Māori chiefs in 1840 ended any chance of his scheme. He moved to Auckland and taught piano until his death in 1864.
de-thierry-hokianga.mechanism: A purchase made at long distance through a go-between meant little once the local chiefs said it did not stand. Those chiefs could allow him to use land, but that gave him no right to rule it.

denmark-buy-california.story:
In February 2025 a satirical online petition called on Denmark to buy the American state of California, as a reply to President Trump's repeated demands for Greenland, a territory of Denmark. In January he had said he did not rule out using military force over Greenland, and Greenland's leader had said his people did not want to be Americans.

The site, Denmarkification, set a goal of crowdfunding $1 trillion, joked about renaming Disneyland and sending Lego executives to negotiate, and argued that Trump would sell because he had called California "the most ruined state in the Union". It collected over 200,000 signatures by its own count, though The Local said that figure might be part of the joke. It took signatures only, not money. Its authors were unknown.

It is on the map as the joke version of a serious question. A petition has no legal force, and its organisers did not claim otherwise.
denmark-buy-california.mechanism: A petition has no legal effect on territory. This one was written to mock the demand to buy Greenland.

du-parquet-islands.story:
Jacques Dyel du Parquet was a French soldier and the governor of Martinique, who in 1650 bought Martinique, Grenada, Saint Lucia and the Grenadines in the Caribbean from the company he served. The Company of the American Islands, which ran these colonies for France, held them from the king and could sell what it held.

Du Parquet was born in Normandy in 1606, and his uncle, Pierre d'Esnambuc, had led the first French colonists in the area. He was sent to Martinique in 1636 and confirmed as governor by the Company of the American Islands the following year. He built a fort and made a truce with the Caribs, the Indigenous islanders, dividing the island between them, and the colony grew to 1,000 men by 1640. He also brought in sugarcane.

The company was collapsing and selling off its rights. The contract was signed in Paris on 27 September 1650, with the king's approval following in August 1651, and the king made du Parquet governor over the islands he now owned. So he held two different things, the land as owner and the office as the king's appointee. Wikipedia's article on him gives the price as 41,500 livres paid in instalments, while its article on the company gives 60,000 livres.

He had already founded settlements on Grenada and Saint Lucia. On Grenada his settlers fought the Indigenous islanders from 1649 until the last resistance was crushed in 1654. He sold Grenada in 1655 to Jean Faudoas, Count of Serillac. On his death in 1658 the king appointed his young son governor of Martinique and Saint Lucia.

The arrangement lasted as long as the Crown allowed. In April 1664 the king revoked all the sales the company had made to private buyers, and a new French West India Company was set up that May. A title bought for cash, with royal approval, could still be undone by a royal decree, because the right to rule had stayed with the king.
du-parquet-islands.mechanism: A private buyer acquired islands and then received the governorship from the king, who kept the final right to rule. The king later cancelled such sales by decree, so ownership lasted only while the Crown allowed it.

firestone-liberia.story:
In 1926 the American tyre maker Firestone won a 99-year lease on up to a million acres of Liberia, in West Africa, at six cents an acre, wherever in the country it chose. That was 4 per cent of Liberia's territory and nearly 10 per cent of its land then considered arable. Liberia was then the only independent country in its region, and it is on the map because it shows how a company can gain great power in a state without any change of borders.

Each side had a reason. Rubber was vital for car tyres, and Britain, then dominating world production, had restricted supply from 1922 under the Stevenson Plan. Harvey Firestone's response was the slogan that America must grow its own rubber. The American government helped search for sites. Liberia's government, for its part, wanted American protection from colonial neighbours eager to annex it.

After the legislature approved a draft, Firestone added a new clause requiring Liberia to take a $5 million loan from his own company, at 7 per cent. The terms matched a 1918 American loan proposal that had aroused objections in Liberia, where critics feared it would make the country an American-run territory, and the new clause set off wide protests. The stated purpose was to pay off more than a million dollars owed to British banks, which might otherwise give Britain a reason to interfere. Firestone also wanted political control to protect a long-term investment. He offered to build a port, which he did not need, to win over the State Department, which wanted one for naval use. Liberia agreed under pressure from the State Department. Two leading Liberian supporters of the bill, a former president and a senator, had by then been hired as Firestone's lawyers.

The terms went well beyond farming. An American financial adviser controlled Liberia's budget, and the country could not borrow without the written consent of Firestone's finance company. The company was largely exempted from present and future taxes. Liberia also promised to help it find labour, and since people in the interior were outside the money economy, this led to forced recruitment. Residents of Harbel were moved away, and in 1929 a local king complained to the legislature that nine towns had been destroyed and that people had to choose between forced labour and emigration.

By 1932 the loan took nearly all government revenue. When Liberia missed a payment, Firestone asked the American government to send a warship, and President Roosevelt refused. So the company could press a government and lobby its own, while force stayed in the hands of the American government, which declined to use it.

Liberia never lost its formal independence. One account calls the result an American protectorate in practice, meaning a country controlled by a stronger one. The company still runs the world's largest contiguous rubber farm, at Harbel.
firestone-liberia.mechanism: Liberia remained independent, but a lease and a loan together gave a company land and a say over state finances. One account calls the result an American protectorate in practice, meaning a country controlled by a stronger one, though Liberia kept its formal right to rule itself.

franco-texian-bill.story:
The Franco-Texian Bill was a proposal in 1841 for the Republic of Texas, then an independent country, to grant three million acres to a private French company. It is on the map as a case in which a government considered handing out land, tax freedom and defence duties to a foreign business.

Two Frenchmen, Jean Pierre Hippolyte Basterrèche and Pierre François de Lassaulx, wanted to set up the Franco Texian Commercial and Colonization Company. The bill was introduced on 12 January 1841. The company was to bring in 8,000 families and build and keep up 20 forts for 20 years. In return it would receive the land, scattered along Texas rivers and not in one block, and its settlers would pay no taxes or tariffs for 20 years. It would also get exclusive trade with the New Mexico settlements and could develop mines, paying Texas 15 per cent of gross returns.

So Texas would have kept the right to rule, while a foreign company held forts, settlers exempt from tax, and sole rights to one line of trade. The French envoy to Texas, Dubois de Saligny, and the Texas politician Sam Houston both supported it, and the Texas House of Representatives approved it on 23 January 1841. It never reached the Senate, because its sponsors saw they could not get the two-thirds majority needed to overcome a threatened veto by acting president David Burnet. As a result nothing was ever built.
franco-texian-bill.mechanism: A cash-poor new state offered land and tax freedom to a foreign company in exchange for settlers and defence. It would have remained Texan territory, and the plan failed in the legislature.

golden-triangle-kings-romans.story:
The Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone is a casino and hotel district on the Mekong River in Bokeo Province, Laos, run by a private company on a long lease. It lies where Laos, Myanmar and Thailand meet, directly across the river from a Thai village. Farmland stood there before, and the people of the village of Ban Kwan were moved to make way.

A special economic zone is an area where a government applies lighter rules to attract investment. In 2007 the Hong Kong-registered Kings Romans Group and the Lao government created this one with the aim of developing a poor region. The company took a 99-year lease on 10,000 hectares, with 3,000 hectares set aside as a duty-free zone.

It draws mostly Chinese visitors. Mandarin is widely spoken, the clocks are set to Beijing time and the Chinese yuan is the usual currency, so some have labelled it a Chinese colony in all but name. The company runs ferries from Thailand, has its own immigration checkpoint on Lao soil and shops, a hospital and apartment blocks. In 2024 the province and the zone's owner, Zhao Wei, opened a new international airport. Bokeo has gone from one of the country's poorest provinces to one of its better off.

In January 2018 the United States Treasury imposed sanctions on the company and on Zhao Wei, accusing them of money laundering and of drug, human and animal trafficking. Zhao Wei denies the accusations. Lao authorities have taken some enforcement action, and shipments of drugs are still reported to pass nearby.

The zone still operates. On paper it is leased land within Laos, under Lao sovereignty, and no declaration of independence has been made.
golden-triangle-kings-romans.mechanism: A lease of this kind leaves the land in Laos while giving a company wide control of what happens there. Laos keeps the legal right to rule, though the place operates much like a separate Chinese-speaking territory.

greece-sell-islands-2010.story:
In March 2010, during Greece's debt crisis, two German members of parliament, Frank Schäffler of the pro-business Free Democrats and Marco Wanderwitz of Chancellor Angela Merkel's Christian Democrats, said the country should sell islands to raise cash. Its budget deficit had reached 12.7 per cent of its economy in 2009, against the European Union's limit of 3 per cent, and opinion polls showed Germans strongly against paying to rescue it.

The newspaper Bild ran the story under the headline "Sell your islands, you bankrupt Greeks! And sell the Acropolis too!" Schäffler said a country that needs to save money must sell its jewellery, so to speak, and privatise. Wanderwitz said Greece should give collateral for any European Union money it received, and that certain islands could serve. Greece's deputy foreign minister, Dimitris Droutsas, said such suggestions were not appropriate.

The remarks named no buyer and no particular island, and they came from individual politicians. It is on the map because of a distinction they blurred. A state can sell government-owned land to a private buyer, and the land stays Greek. Selling the right to rule it, so that it left Greece, would be a transfer of territory, and a government cannot be made to do so.
greece-sell-islands-2010.mechanism: A proposal of this kind has no legal effect unless the state that holds the land agrees to sell. Greece dismissed the idea.

greenland-purchase-offers.story:
The United States has tried several times to buy Greenland, the Arctic island that belongs to the Kingdom of Denmark and governs itself. Buying territory from another state has real precedents, including the American purchase of Alaska in 1867.

Secretary of State William Seward backed a purchase in 1867, the same year as Alaska, and there were talks again in 1910. In 1946 the United States secretly offered Denmark $100 million in gold, which Denmark rejected. In 2019 President Trump said he wanted to buy the island, and Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen called the idea absurd and said Greenland was not for sale.

In his second term from 2025 Trump pressed again and spoke of tariffs against Denmark. In January 2026 Greenland's leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen said Greenland would choose Denmark, and reports put opposition to an American takeover at 85 percent of Greenlanders.

The law has changed since the earlier offers. An offer in 1946 went to the Danish government. Under Greenland's Self-Government Act, independence is for the Greenlandic people to decide, followed by negotiation with Denmark and a referendum. So a sale over the heads of the people living there would run against the law that governs the island.

On 22 September 2026 the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a security agreement in New York with no expiry date. It expands the American military presence and bars countries outside NATO, the Western military alliance, from setting up military installations. Frederiksen said it recognises Denmark's sovereignty, meaning its legal right to rule the island, and the Greenlandic people's right to decide their own future. No sale has taken place.

The agreement gave the United States a larger military presence with no change of ownership.
greenland-purchase-offers.mechanism: A state cannot be made to sell its territory, so a purchase needs the seller's agreement. In Greenland's case, the law also leaves the decision on independence to the people who live there.

herm-lease.story:
Herm is a tiny island in the Channel Islands, about a mile and a half long, part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a self-governing territory under the British Crown. It is on the map because its right of use has been traded for over a century, while the ownership stayed with a government.

A lease is a right to use land for a fixed time in return for payment, and when the time runs out the land goes back to the owner. Prince Gebhard Blücher, a German noble, leased Herm from the British government in 1889 and brought in wallabies, which lasted until 1910. The novelist Compton Mackenzie took over the tenancy in 1920 and recalled numerous practical problems during his three years there. Percival Perry was tenant from 1923 to 1939. During the Second World War German troops used the beaches for practice landings and left little behind.

The States of Guernsey, the island's government, bought Herm from the Crown in 1949 so that local people and tourists could enjoy it, and let it to Major Peter Wood, who restored the run-down island with his wife over 30 years. In 2008 his daughter and her husband put the remaining 40 years of their lease up for sale, asking £15 million. A trust called Starboard Settlement bought it for considerably less and formed Herm Island Ltd to run the island.

Talks on a 21-year extension broke down in 2013, with the tenant offering £440,000 and the States of Guernsey asking for £6 million. In 2023 the lease was extended to 2069 for an undisclosed sum, and Herm Island Ltd still runs the island. Throughout all of this Guernsey's laws applied and its government stayed the landlord, so no buyer ever gained any right to govern.
herm-lease.mechanism: What was sold was a lease, a right to use land for a fixed time. The government of Guernsey kept ownership, and each tenant had to bargain with it to extend.

herzl-palestine-offer.story:
Theodor Herzl, one of the founders of Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, tried in 1896 and 1901 to get Palestine from the Ottoman Empire, which ruled it. The empire was deeply in debt to European powers, whose representatives controlled much of its revenue through a body called the Ottoman Public Debt Administration. The case is on the map as an attempt to buy territory directly from a government, using that debt as the lever.

According to an account published by the Turkish public broadcaster TRT World, he offered £20 million in 1896 for a charter allowing Jews to settle there, a sum that account says would have covered about a fifth of the debt. A charter is a formal grant of rights from a ruler. He worked through intermediaries named Philip de Newlinski and Arminius Vambery, who doubted that Jerusalem could be sold whatever the state of Ottoman finances.

Sultan Abdul Hamid II refused, telling Newlinski that he could not sell even a foot of land because it belonged to his people, who had won the empire with their blood. As ruler and caliph he also drew authority from holding Islam's holy places. Herzl met the sultan in person in 1901 with a different proposal, a company of Jewish financiers in Istanbul that would buy up Ottoman debt over time, in return for autonomy for some land in Palestine as a destination for Jewish migrants. Autonomy means limited self-rule inside a larger state, which is less than the charter he had first sought.

The sultan was interested in consolidating the debt but treated it as a separate matter from settlement, so nothing came of the land proposal. The £20 million figure rests on that one account.
herzl-palestine-offer.mechanism: Part of a state can be sold only if its ruler agrees, and the sultan refused even while in debt. Herzl's later plan offered debt relief as the price and asked for autonomy, or limited self-rule, instead of full control.

hospitaller-caribbean-1651.story:
From 1651 to 1665 the Knights of Malta, a Catholic military order, owned four Caribbean islands: Saint Christopher (now Saint Kitts), Saint Croix, Saint Barthélemy and Saint Martin. The order, also called the Knights Hospitaller, was at that time made up mostly of French aristocrats, and many of its members held posts in French colonial service. It is on the map as a rare case of a religious order buying colonies.

They came to the order through Phillippe de Poincy, a knight who went to Saint Christopher in 1639 as governor for the Company of the American Islands, the French company then running the colonies. King Louis XIII soon made him Lieutenant-General for the whole Caribbean. He expanded French settlement to the other islands and agreed with the Dutch the boundary on Saint Martin that still exists. He also ruled as he liked. He treated resisters harshly, clashed with Capuchin missionaries and paid for his grand style of living with income from the order's estates in Europe.

The company tried to replace him. It sent a new man, Noël de Thoisy, with an order from the king, and Poincy's militia drove him off the island and later sent him to France in chains. To keep his post, Poincy suggested in 1649 that the order buy the islands. The company was failing, and Cardinal Mazarin, France's chief minister, was busy elsewhere. It dissolved in 1651, selling its rights.

Under a treaty with France two years later the king kept the final right to rule. The knights had full civil and religious authority, could send only French knights as governors, and owed a gold crown worth 1,000 écus to each new king. The buyer therefore held the land and local government, while the monarch held sovereignty, the ultimate right to rule. Poincy ruled until his death in 1660 and built forts and a grand residence.

A rebellion overthrew the order's rule on Saint Croix in 1657 and Caribs attacked Saint Barthélemy. The colonies made no profit and the order still owed France part of the purchase price. Under pressure from the French minister Colbert it sold them in 1665 to the new French West India Company.
hospitaller-caribbean-1651.mechanism: A religious order bought islands from a bankrupt company. It held ownership and full local government, while the French king kept the final right to rule.

huang-nubo-grimsstadir.story:
In 2011 Huang Nubo, a Chinese businessman who founded the property firm Zhongkun Group, tried to buy about 300 square kilometres of wilderness at Grímsstaðir á Fjöllum in north-eastern Iceland, equal to 0.3 per cent of the country. He offered about $10 million for the land, which was partly owned by the government, and planned to spend about $200 million on a tourist resort and what he described as Europe's biggest nature reserve. Iceland was then recovering from its financial crisis, and some saw the investment as useful outside the capital region.

Icelandic law bars large land purchases by people or companies from outside the European Economic Area, a group of European countries that share a single market. So he needed an exemption from the minister. Interior Minister Ögmundur Jónasson refused in late 2011. He said an exemption would make the law meaningless and could encourage others to buy up large parts of Iceland, and he stressed that the buyer was a company, Huang's Zhongkun. Parties split, with the Social Democrats leaning toward the deal and the minister's Left Greens opposed. One Social Democrat member of parliament called the decision crazy, deplorable and devastating, and said there were at least 25 precedents.

Huang called the minister a racist. In May 2012 a committee of three ministries recommended a smaller deal, a 40-year lease of two to three square kilometres for a hotel and tourist facilities. Huang had said that building one hotel did not interest him. The lease is not known to have been signed.

The bid never touched the question of who rules the land, since a buyer would have held it under Icelandic law. It shows that a state can stop a sale at the earlier stage, by controlling who may own land at all.
huang-nubo-grimsstadir.mechanism: A country can limit who may buy its land by nationality, and here a minister refused to waive that limit. The bid concerned land ownership only, and the right to rule the land was never on offer.

isle-of-man-revestment.story:
The Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea, was for a long time ruled under the Crown by a noble family, as its feudal lord, until the family sold those rights to the British government. Under feudalism, land and the power to govern it could be held as a kind of inherited property, granted by a monarch.

A 1609 Act of Parliament gave the rights of Lord of Man to William Stanley, 6th Earl of Derby, and his heirs, and they came down to the Dukes of Atholl. An act passed in 1726 had already authorised the Treasury to make a purchase. Because Parliament had fixed the rights by law, it took another Act to end them. Under a contract with the Treasury, Charlotte, Duchess of Atholl, sold the rights to the Crown for £70,000, and the Isle of Man Purchase Act of 1765, also called the Act of Revestment, put this into effect on 10 May that year. Payment was due by 1 June.

The word revestment means putting something back into its earlier holder, here the Crown. Plans to merge the island into the English county of Cumberland met fierce local resistance, led by Sir George Moore, Speaker of the House of Keys, a chamber of the island's parliament, and did not go ahead.

The family kept its rights as local landlord, its power to choose the bishop and other privileges. Those went later under an Act of 1825, and they sold for £417,144 in 1828. It shows that ruling rights could once be bought like property, but only because a higher authority, Parliament, had defined them and agreed to the transfer.
isle-of-man-revestment.mechanism: Here a state bought ruling rights from a private family. The sale needed an Act of Parliament because an earlier Act had created those rights.

jarch-capital-south-sudan.story:
In January 2009 Philippe Heilberg, a former Wall Street banker who chaired the New York firm Jarch Capital, said he had secured leasehold rights, the right to use land for a fixed time, to 400,000 hectares in south Sudan, an area the size of Dubai. South Sudan was then an autonomous region of Sudan after a long civil war. The land was remote, bordering the Nile with no tarred roads. Jarch's board included former American diplomats and intelligence officials.

The unusual part is who he dealt with. Most land deals of the time were with governments. Heilberg took a majority stake in a company controlled by Gabriel Matip, the son of Paulino Matip, a warlord who had fought on both sides of Sudan's civil war and became deputy commander of the southern army after a 2005 peace deal. In his words, you have to go to the guns. The deal ran through an affiliate in the Virgin Islands, and he refused to say what he paid. The Financial Times called it post-colonial Africa's biggest private land deal, second only to Daewoo's in Madagascar.

He was betting on borders. Heilberg said that Sudan and possibly Nigeria, Ethiopia and Somalia would break apart, and that being in early on such shifts in sovereignty would pay off. He said he was also in contact with rebels in Darfur, Ethiopian dissidents and the government of the breakaway state of Somaliland. He had no farming expertise and planned to find partners to cultivate the land.

Land law in the south was vague, and experts and regional officials doubted he could enforce his rights. South Sudan did become independent in 2011. Whether the lease was ever enforced is not known.
jarch-capital-south-sudan.mechanism: A private investor bought rights from an armed commander instead of a government, hoping a future state would honour them. Such a deal gives no right to rule, and its value depends on who ends up in power.

johnson-v-mintosh.story:
Johnson v. M'Intosh is an 1823 United States Supreme Court case that set the rule on private people buying land from Native American nations. It remains the law and is the first case many American law students read in their property courses. It is on the map because it answers the question of whether someone can get land by buying it directly from the people who live there, with no government involved.

Thomas Johnson, later a Supreme Court justice, had bought land from the Piankeshaw in 1773 and 1775. People claiming through his heirs sued William McIntosh, who held a federal land patent, a government deed, to what they said was the same land. Evidence suggests the two tracts did not actually overlap, and that the parties knew this and misstated the facts to get a ruling. A court in Illinois dismissed the claim because the Piankeshaw could not transfer the land.

Chief Justice John Marshall, writing for a unanimous Supreme Court, upheld the dismissal. He surveyed how European powers had taken land in the Americas and set out the doctrine of discovery. Under it, a European power gained sovereignty, the ultimate legal right, over land it discovered, along with the sole right to buy out the Indigenous occupants. The occupants kept only a right to occupy the land. When the United States became independent, it inherited that sole right from Britain.

Put simply, the Piankeshaw could live on their land and sell it to one buyer only, the federal government. A deed from them to anyone else gave no valid title. Courts call this rule inalienability, meaning the right cannot be transferred. Because there was only one lawful buyer, one commentator has noted, there was no bidding between settlers, which let the government acquire Native lands at the lowest cost.

Most of what Marshall wrote about discovery went beyond what the case needed. The firm holding is the bar on selling. Law teachers now commonly present the reasoning critically, with a leading casebook calling it discomforting and quoting the view that it rested on a Eurocentric belief in Indian inferiority. It remains good law all the same, cited by lower courts several times a year, and it is the basis of the law of aboriginal title, the rights Indigenous peoples keep over their land. Similar rules shaped early cases in Australia, Canada and New Zealand.

Even a fair payment to the people who have lived on the land for generations will not create ownership that an American court accepts.
johnson-v-mintosh.mechanism: Private citizens could not buy land from Native American nations, because only the sovereign, the government with the right to rule, could acquire it. The rule made the state the only lawful buyer, whatever price or agreement a private person might reach.

lanai-ellison.story:
Lānaʻi is the sixth-largest Hawaiian island, 364 square kilometres, and 98 per cent of it belongs to Larry Ellison, co-founder of the software firm Oracle. He bought that share in June 2012 for $300 million. The other 2 per cent, including the harbour and the homes of about 3,400 residents, belongs to the state or to homeowners. It is on the map because people often imagine that owning nearly a whole island makes someone its ruler.

Single owners have held most of the island for over a century. Walter Gibson came to reorganise a Mormon settlement and bought land there for $3,000 in 1863 with church money. He titled it in his own name and was excommunicated, but he kept the land, and by the 1870s he held most of the island for ranching. His family's sugar company failed in 1901 after bringing in nearly 800 labourers. By 1907 the rancher Charles Gay owned about half. A law barred the territorial government from selling him so much land, so he got the rest by swapping some Honolulu land for it, then mortgaged the island for $200,000 and lost it.

James Dole bought the island in 1922 and made it the world's largest pineapple plantation. It passed to David Murdock in 1985 when he bought the parent company. Ellison has spent an estimated $450 million remodelling the island's Four Seasons resort, which reopened in 2016.

An owner of this kind has great practical power over jobs, housing and business on the island. Lānaʻi has been part of Maui County since Hawaii became a state in 1959, and it has no separate legal status.
lanai-ellison.mechanism: Almost a whole island can be private property while it remains an ordinary part of a county and a US state. The owner controls land, jobs and resorts, and no separate jurisdiction arises from that.

liberia-cape-mesurado.story:
Liberia, in West Africa, grew from land acquired by a private American organisation, the American Colonization Society, which raised money to send free Black Americans to Africa. In the early 1800s free Black people in the United States faced severe legal discrimination and were not treated as citizens. Some opponents of slavery hoped emigration would help them. Slaveholders wanted free Black people out of their states, believing they threatened the stability of slave societies.

Its first ship left New York in 1820, with agents sent to find a site. In December 1821 they acquired Cape Mesurado, a 36-mile strip near present-day Monrovia, from a local ruler, King Peter, perhaps under some threat of force. The United States declined requests to make Liberia a colony or a formal protectorate, though it would intervene at times when Liberia's territory was threatened.

The colonists were attacked by the peoples whose territory it was, and suffered from disease and hunger. Only 1,819 of the 4,571 emigrants who arrived between 1820 and 1843 survived, the highest settler death rate reported in modern records. The colony spread along the coast and inland, sometimes by force, and other American colonisation societies set up their own settlements. These joined as the Commonwealth of Liberia in 1838.

Under its first Black governor, Joseph Jenkins Roberts, Liberians voted in a referendum for independence, and eleven signers declared it on 26 July 1847. The society and some state governments continued to send money and emigrants into the 1870s. Roberts became the first president.

Liberia kept its independence through the European scramble for Africa. The descendants of the settlers, called Americo-Liberians, a small minority, controlled the country's politics until a violent overthrow in 1980, followed by two civil wars. It is one of the few cases of a private land purchase ending in a recognised state. Its settlers came to rule the peoples already living there.
liberia-cape-mesurado.mechanism: A private society obtained land from a local ruler and governed it as a colony, and the settlers later declared a state. The colony expanded at times by force against the people already living there.

liechtenstein-purchase.story:
Liechtenstein, the small country between Switzerland and Austria, began as a purchase. It was not won by conquest and did not come out of a peace treaty. The Liechtenstein family were very rich nobles whose estates lay in Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia and Austria, inside the lands of the Habsburg dynasty. Their reason lay in how the Holy Roman Empire worked. The emperor had made the head of the family an imperial prince in 1620, but only rulers of land held directly under the emperor could sit and vote in the Imperial Diet, the assembly of the empire.

The family therefore needed a territory of that kind. The lordship of Schellenberg and the county of Vaduz, in the Alpine Rhine Valley, qualified. They were badly run and in debt under the counts of Hohenems, and an imperial commission decided they should be sold to clear those debts. Prince Johann Adam Andreas outbid the other interested parties and paid 115,000 guilders for Schellenberg, well above its value, with the handover ceremony in 1699.

Schellenberg alone was judged too small to earn a seat, so the deal included first refusal on Vaduz, which he bought for 290,000 guilders in 1712. Vaduz's men swore allegiance only after being promised that their old rights would continue. In 1719 Emperor Charles VI joined the two lands into the Principality of Liechtenstein. No ruling prince visited until 1842.

It became a sovereign state in 1806, when Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine took it out of the empire. The family still reigns there today.

What made the purchase work was a higher authority, the emperor, who approved the sale and could turn land into a principality.
liechtenstein-purchase.mechanism: A family bought land from an indebted count with the emperor's approval, and the emperor then raised it to a principality. Land and ruling rights both passed because the emperor agreed, and full independence came in 1806 when the empire was breaking up.

luderitz-angra-pequena.story:
German South West Africa, now Namibia, began with purchases by a merchant from Bremen, Adolf Lüderitz. Angra Pequena is a bay on the dry Atlantic coast, now the town of Lüderitz. In May 1883 he bought the anchorage and the land 8 kilometres around it from Josef Frederiks II, a chief of Bethanie, for £100 in gold and 200 rifles. Frederiks cared about fertile land, and the shore had little value to his people.

In August Lüderitz bought a coastal strip between the Orange River and Angra Pequena for £500 and 60 rifles. The contract gave the width as 20 geographical miles. A German geographical mile is about 7.4 kilometres, while the mile used locally was the English mile of 1.6 kilometres. So the strip was 140 kilometres wide, against the roughly 32 that a reader using English miles would expect. Both Lüderitz and the missionary who witnessed the deal, Johannes Bam, knew that Frederiks did not understand the difference. He had sold nearly all his people's land. His complaint to the German government was never delivered, because the official carrying it, Gustav Nachtigal, died on the way home. Germans called the deal the Mile Swindle.

A merchant's deed needed a government behind it. Chancellor Otto von Bismarck at first held back, fearing the cost of defending far-off land. As the 1884 election approached he changed course and asked London repeatedly about Britain's intentions, with no answer. When Britain moved to take the coast, he declared protection, avoiding the word colony for diplomatic reasons, and the German flag went up on 7 August 1884.

Lüderitz kept buying from other chiefs until he held an area of 580,000 square kilometres on paper, but found no gold or diamonds and ran out of money. In April 1885 he sold everything to the German Colonial Society for 500,000 marks, and he died the next year. In 1887 even the Foreign Office's own colonial department doubted the treaty's validity.
luderitz-angra-pequena.mechanism: A merchant's private land deals became the basis for a colony only when his government chose to declare protection over them. A chief sold land under terms he had been misled about, and the German Foreign Office itself later doubted the treaty's validity.

lundy-harman.story:
Lundy is a small English island in the Bristol Channel, about 5 kilometres long and 19 kilometres off the coast of Devon, which has often been privately owned. The name comes from Old Norse and means puffin island. It had 28 residents in 2007. The businessman Martin Coles Harman bought it from the Christie family in 1924, along with its mail contract and a boat.

In 1929 he issued his own coins, the Half Puffin and the One Puffin, set equal in value to the British halfpenny and penny and named after the bird. Puffin stamps, sold as local carriage labels, remain a collector's item on the island.

Because Lundy was part of England, he was prosecuted under the Coinage Act of 1870. Devon magistrates fined him £5 with £15 15 shillings in costs in April 1930. He appealed to the High Court in 1931 and lost. The coins were withdrawn and became collector's items.

Harman owned the island and still could not issue money there. The island was bought in 1969 by the millionaire Jack Hayward, who gave it to the National Trust, a British conservation charity. The Landmark Trust now manages it and pays for it through day trips and holiday lets.
lundy-harman.mechanism: Buying an island brings ownership of the land, and national law still applies there. Harman's conviction showed that a private owner cannot issue money in a place that remains part of the state.

manhattan-new-netherland.story:
Manhattan, now part of New York City, is famous as the island said to have been bought from the Lenape, its Indigenous people, in 1626 for $24 worth of beads. The buyer was Peter Minuit, director of the colony of New Netherland for the Dutch West India Company, a trading company chartered in the Netherlands. It is on the map as the best-known story of buying land from Indigenous people.

Very little is known about the deal. It rests on two sentences in a single letter of November 1626 by Pieter Schagen, a company board member, who gave the price as 60 guilders of trade goods. The site of the deal is unknown. A New York historian turned this into $24 in 1844, probably wrongly, and one Amsterdam institute put it at about $1,000 in 2006 money. The goods are not recorded, though a similar deal for nearby Staten Island involved cloth, kettles, axe heads and hoes.

The two sides may have meant very different things. The company treated the payment as buying land outright. Research cited by New York City's Landmarks Preservation Commission suggests the Lenape probably understood the deal as temporary, closer to a lease, and may have seen the 60 guilders as a ceremonial gift sealing an agreement to share use of the land. The only written record is a Dutch letter.

Manhattan became the site of the Dutch town of New Amsterdam. The Dutch understanding is the one that shaped what came after.
manhattan-new-netherland.mechanism: A trading company treated a payment as buying land outright, while the sellers may have understood it as sharing use. What passed depends on which side's understanding is taken, and the only written record is a Dutch letter.

menier-anticosti.story:
Anticosti is a 7,943-square-kilometre island in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, Canada, larger than Prince Edward Island, that was bought in 1895 by Henri Menier, the French chocolate millionaire. It had been granted as a seigneury, or feudal estate, to the explorer Louis Jolliet in 1680. A Montreal land company went bankrupt trying to settle it in 1872, and Francis Stockwell, an English businessman who paid $101,000 at auction in 1884, went bankrupt too.

Menier wanted a private sports preserve and hoped to make the island a self-supporting estate. He brought in foxes, bison, moose and 220 white-tailed deer, whose descendants now number over 100,000. He built a model village at Baie-Sainte-Claire and in 1900 moved the settlement to Port-Menier, which had a long wharf and a sawmill.

He held the island as private land in Canada. He died in 1913 and the island was sold in 1926 to a pulp and paper company. The Quebec government bought it in 1974, and most of its 200 or so people live in Port-Menier today.
menier-anticosti.mechanism: A foreign buyer could own a whole Canadian island and run it as a personal estate, but it stayed under Canadian law. It ended in public ownership when Quebec bought it.

new-zealand-company.story:
The New Zealand Company was a British colonising company that claimed to have bought about a third of New Zealand from Māori in 1839. It followed the plan of Edward Gibbon Wakefield, who proposed buying land cheaply from Indigenous people and reselling it at a high price to settlers, using the difference to pay for shipping emigrants and to give shareholders a profit. Under this plan, emigrants were divided into capitalists and labourers, and labourers had to work for several years before getting land of their own.

The whole scheme depended on buying directly from Māori. In March 1839 the promoters learned that a government bill would allow land to be bought only from the government, which would have ruined them. Wakefield told them to possess themselves of the soil before others did, and they rushed to act. They bought the ship Tory and sent it out on 12 May under Colonel William Wakefield, with £3,000 of goods for barter. The company was already selling land in London, sight unseen, at £1 an acre, and by the end of July it had sold every section for its first settlement, before anyone knew the ship had arrived. The government warned it that title bought from Māori carried no guarantee and would probably be open to repurchase by the Crown.

Wakefield offered guns, tools and clothing around what is now Wellington, and by November had marks on deeds that supposedly covered 20 million acres, at about a halfpenny an acre. The company promised that one section in ten would be reserved for Māori, scattered among the settlers. The company's interpreter, Barrett, told an inquiry in 1843 that he had said to the chiefs that when they signed, the gentlemen in England might know who the chiefs were.

The 1840 Treaty of Waitangi then gave the British Crown the sole right to buy Māori land, and Governor Hobson began reviewing all earlier sales. A land commission under William Spain, set up by the Colonial Office, found three serious flaws in the Wellington deal. Chiefs of three villages at the settlement site had been neither consulted nor paid, one young chief had sold land he did not control, and the terms had been badly explained. A disputed purchase in the Wairau Valley led in 1843 to a clash in which 22 settlers and four Māori died.

Financial trouble began that year. The company returned its charter, granted in 1840, in 1850 and closed in 1858, having founded Wellington, Nelson, Wanganui and Dunedin. Those towns are still there today.
new-zealand-company.mechanism: A private company tried to buy land before the state arrived, and the treaty then made the Crown the only lawful buyer. Its deeds were reviewed and could not stand on their own.

niihau-robinson.story:
Niʻihau is the seventh largest Hawaiian island, 180 square kilometres, lying about 29 kilometres west of Kauaʻi. It has been privately owned by one family since a Scottish plantation owner, Elizabeth Sinclair, bought it from King Kamehameha V of Hawaii in 1864. She paid $10,000 in gold, a price that also covered parts of the island of Kauaʻi. It is on the map as a Hawaiian island closed to most outsiders by its private owners.

Ownership passed to her descendants, the Robinson family, and brothers Bruce and Keith Robinson now manage it. The seller was the monarch of the then independent Kingdom of Hawaii. Hawaii later became part of the United States, and the family's private title carried through that change, so Niʻihau is counted within Kauaʻi County.

The family's rules keep the island closed to outsiders apart from relatives, US Navy personnel, officials and invited guests, which has earned it the name the Forbidden Isle and some controversy. Supervised tours and hunting trips have been allowed since 1987. Its residents, mostly Native Hawaiians, speak Hawaiian as their first language. The census counted 170 people in 2010 and 84 in 2020.

The arrangement can look like a private state, and in law it is not one. The census counts the people there and the United States Navy comes and goes. Control over who lands comes from property rights.
niihau-robinson.mechanism: A monarch sold the land, and the family has kept it through the change from kingdom to United States rule. Ownership gives the family the power to control who enters, but no separate right to rule the island.

nile-trading-mukaya.story:
Nile Trading & Development is a Texas company that in March 2008 signed a 49-year lease over about 600,000 hectares in Mukaya Payam, a district of Lainya County in what is now South Sudan, for $25,000. South Sudan was then still part of Sudan.

According to the Oakland Institute, a California research group that published the contract, the lease gave unrestricted rights to exploit all natural resources on the land, with the possibility of nearly a million acres more. It is on the map as an example of how much a lease can claim for a small sum.

After the Institute's report spread in 2011, the year South Sudan became independent, the community learned of the deal and mobilised against it. Chiefs and county authorities protested in July, and in August a committee of chiefs, state legislators and officials went to the capital, Juba, to reject the lease before President Salva Kiir. Kiir replied that the matter should be settled according to their will. The Institute announced that the deal had been effectively stalled. Whether it was ever formally cancelled is not known.
nile-trading-mukaya.mechanism: A lease signed before South Sudan's independence gave a foreign firm wide rights for a small price. It gave the firm no right to rule, and local opposition reached the president.

palmyra-fullard-leo.story:
Palmyra is an uninhabited coral atoll in the central Pacific, about 1,000 miles south of Hawaii, made up of 33 islets with about 600 acres of dry land and a large submerged reef. It has been bought and sold by private owners while also being claimed by governments, which makes it a good place to see that owning land and ruling it are two separate things.

American visitors tried to claim it in 1859 under the Guano Islands Act, a law on claiming islands that hold guano, or bird droppings, used as fertiliser. It had none, so the claims were abandoned. In 1862 King Kamehameha IV of Hawaii commissioned two Hawaiian citizens, Zenas Bent and Johnson Wilkinson, to take possession. The Kingdom of Hawaii annexed it on 15 April and the two became its joint owners. So one act gave a kingdom the right to rule and gave two men the ownership. Their shares were then sold and inherited many times, through a widow's four heirs, a navigation company and others. In 1922 Henry Cooper sold his interest to Leslie and Ellen Fullard-Leo for $15,000, and they set up a company to harvest coconuts.

The atoll came under the United States when Hawaii did. The family tried from 1937 to lease it to the Navy, but during the talks the federal government sued them, claiming that the atoll had never been lawfully private property. The Navy occupied it and built a runway during the Second World War. The case reached the US Supreme Court as United States v. Fullard-Leo, and in 1947 the Court ruled for the Fullard-Leo and Cooper families, which confirmed their private title against the government. This did not make Palmyra independent of the United States in any way. The government that lost as a claimant to ownership remained the government.

It is now the only incorporated US territory, meaning one fully under the Constitution and permanently American, with no resident government. The Interior Department administers it.

The family later turned down offers to use the atoll as a nuclear waste dump or a casino, according to the Nature Conservancy, a conservation charity, which bought most of the land from them in 2000 for $30 million. Palmyra is now a federal wildlife refuge, and researchers work there in a station the charity opened in 2005.
palmyra-fullard-leo.mechanism: Owning land and governing it are separate things. The family won clear private ownership against the federal government in court, and the atoll stayed under United States rule throughout.

poyais.story:
Poyais was a country that did not exist, sold to British investors and settlers in the 1820s by a Scottish adventurer named Gregor MacGregor. It is on the map as the classic fraud of its kind.

MacGregor had fought in the Venezuelan war of independence and briefly seized Amelia Island in Florida. On 29 April 1820 he persuaded George Frederic Augustus, the Mosquito King, an Indigenous ruler on the Caribbean coast of what is now Honduras, to grant him and his heirs about 8 million acres in exchange for rum and jewellery. That grant was real, and he registered it in a London court in 1822. The land was undeveloped jungle, fit for little farming.

Back in London he called himself the Cazique, or prince, of Poyais. He described a prosperous nation with a capital, St Joseph, of up to 20,000 people, an opera house, a healthy climate and rivers holding gold. A 355-page guidebook under the name of a Captain Thomas Strangeways appeared in 1822, along with maps and documents, a flag and banknotes printed in Scotland. Almost all of it was invented. The slow speed of news and the unsettled politics of South America helped convince people. He sold land certificates at 2 shillings and 3 pence an acre, about £11 for 100 acres, plus military commissions and government posts. A London firm underwrote a £200,000 loan at 6 per cent.

Two ships took about 250 settlers out. The Honduras Packet left London on 10 September 1822 with about 70 people, and the Kennersley Castle left Leith on 22 January 1823 with almost 200. They found only some old foundations and rubble. Their ship's captain sailed off, the man in charge left repeatedly, and the rainy season brought insects, malaria and yellow fever. In May 1823 a passing schooner carried word that Poyais did not exist. The Mosquito king revoked the grant. Survivors were taken to Belize in three trips, and disease killed many more. At least 180 of the roughly 250 died, and fewer than 50 returned to Britain.

The London press attacked MacGregor, and even so six survivors signed a statement in October 1823 blaming his agents and not him. By then the bonds were trading under a tenth of their face value. He moved to Paris and sold Poyais again to French investors. In 1826 a French court tried him and three others for fraud, and it convicted only one associate. He then ran smaller schemes in London for about a decade. He moved to Venezuela in 1838, died in Caracas in 1845 and was buried with military honours. He was never convicted of the fraud.
poyais.mechanism: A land grant from a local ruler was the one real element, and the rest was invented. Buyers paid for land and posts in a state that existed only in MacGregor's documents.
poyais.why: The death toll is stated as at least 180 of about 250, from Wikipedia's account. The earlier figure of two-thirds came from History.com. The two are close but not the same.

puertopia-sol.story:
Puertopia, later renamed Sol, was a plan by wealthy cryptocurrency investors to build a new city in Puerto Rico, a US territory, in which the money would be virtual and contracts public. They arrived after Hurricane Maria hit in September 2017, as cryptocurrency prices were soaring. Their leader was Brock Pierce, director of the Bitcoin Foundation and co-founder of the blockchain firm Block.One.

The attraction was a tax rule. Americans who move to Puerto Rico can pay no federal personal income tax or capital gains tax, without giving up their citizenship. One member said they chose the island because the storm had swept everything away, leaving a case for rebuilding, and another investor called it a godsend in the long term.

In early 2018 they rented a 20,000-square-foot hotel in the capital, called the Monastery, as their base, and toured properties where they could have their own airports and docks. They debated buying the Roosevelt Roads Naval Station, 9,000 acres with two deep-water ports. Another resident said they had told him they would buy 250,000 acres and incorporate their own city. Some members thought moving into Old San Juan was enough. For the time being the governor was willing to speak at their conference, and they said they were close to permission for a cryptocurrency bank.

Their idea of a city was limited by law from the start, because the island remains under United States law. A local critic spoke of crypto colonialism, and another Puerto Rican called the island a tax playground for the rich. They are not known to have bought the base or founded a city.
puertopia-sol.mechanism: Puerto Rico's tax rules can be used without any land deal, and buying land there brings no separate sovereignty, because the island remains under United States law. The investors' plan relied on those rules and on local government goodwill.

ras-el-hekma.story:
Ras El-Hekma is a stretch of Egypt's Mediterranean coast about 350 kilometres north-west of Cairo. In February 2024 the governments of Egypt and the United Arab Emirates signed a $35 billion agreement over it, with the Emirates represented by a consortium led by ADQ, a state investment fund based in Abu Dhabi. It is on the map because of the size of the deal and the question of what such a payment actually buys.

The money came in two parts. ADQ was to pay $24 billion for the rights to develop the area, and to convert $11 billion of deposits it held into investments in projects elsewhere in Egypt. The plan covers more than 170 million square metres, or about 170 square kilometres, to be built up as a holiday destination, financial centre and free zone, an area with special business and tax rules. Egypt keeps a 35 per cent stake in the development. The UAE's investment minister described it as support for Egypt's economy.

What passed here is development rights, the right to build on and profit from land, with Egypt as a partner. The announcement does not mention handing over the right to rule.
ras-el-hekma.mechanism: The buyer acquired development rights over land in Egypt, and Egypt kept a share of the project. The announcement describes an investment and does not mention handing over the right to rule the land.

red-river-selkirk.story:
The Red River Colony was a settlement scheme around present-day Winnipeg in Canada, on a block of land five times the size of Scotland that a private company gave to one nobleman. Thomas Douglas, Earl of Selkirk, was troubled by the eviction of Scottish farmers in the Highland Clearances and believed emigration was their best hope. After reading the explorer Alexander MacKenzie's account of the region, he spent years on the idea, founding two other farm colonies that failed.

The Hudson's Bay Company held the region under a royal charter, and two fur companies dominated it. The company refused him in 1802. By 1807 Selkirk saw that he needed one of the big fur companies on his side. In 1811 the Hudson's Bay Company granted him 300,000 square kilometres out of its own territory, known as the Selkirk Concession or Assiniboia. It expected the colony to grow flour, beef and butter for its fur trade and cut the cost of shipping supplies from Britain. In return he promised 200 men a year for the company and agreed to keep the colony out of the fur trade. Selkirk bought many company shares in 1811 and 1812, and historians have debated how far that explains the grant.

The rival North West Company opposed the colony, and the conflict turned violent. In 1816 the colony's governor, Robert Semple, and about 20 settlers were killed at the Battle of Seven Oaks, and the settlement was abandoned for a time. Selkirk arrived the next year with about 100 disbanded soldiers and captured the rival's headquarters at Fort William.

The land south of the 49th parallel passed to the United States under an 1818 treaty. The colony existed until 1870, when the Hudson's Bay territory went to Canada.
