Selkirk held land under a company that held its rights from the Crown, so he never had any independence to claim.
red-river-selkirk.mechanism: A chartered company, one given its rights by the Crown, could pass part of its land to a private person. The grant gave him land under the company's charter and no independence from Britain.

romanov-empire-bakov.story:
The Romanov Empire is a self-declared country, or micronation, with no land of its own, started in 2011 by Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman and former member of the Russian parliament from Yekaterinburg. He is chairman of a small monarchist party, and he says the project restores the Russian Empire. A writer once called him a political Leonardo for a run of unusual projects, including a local currency called the Ural franc.

The project began as the Imperial Throne. In 2014 it issued a manifesto naming the German prince Karl Emich of Leiningen as Emperor Nicholas III, and in 2017 it took the name Romanov Empire, with Bakov as Archchancellor. It sold passports online for 1,000 rubles, about $31, and claimed to have issued about 4,000 by 2014. In July 2013 Bakov said his state had granted citizenship to Edward Snowden, the former US intelligence contractor, who was then staying in Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow.

To become a real state the project needed territory, so Bakov talked with several countries about buying land. As of 2017, talks with Kiribati and the Gambia had failed. Nicholas III also wrote to Vladimir Putin asking for land in Yekaterinburg for a capital, and that request was denied. A land purchase alone would bring private ownership only, unless the seller also gave up the right to rule.

In 2020 Bakov said a successor project called Arca Noë would be based on a floating settlement in neutral Mediterranean waters near Venice. It is not known to have been built.
romanov-empire-bakov.mechanism: A private buyer needs a government willing to give up part of its territory, and the governments approached did not agree.

rudd-concession.story:
The Rudd Concession was an 1888 agreement in which King Lobengula of Matabeleland, in what is now Zimbabwe, signed away the mineral rights of his kingdom to three men, Charles Rudd, Francis Thompson and Rochfort Maguire, who were agents of the businessman and politician Cecil Rhodes. Rhodes wanted to bring the region into the British Empire, and he needed the concession to win a charter for a company that could annex and govern it. It is on the map as the case of a narrow mining paper turning into a whole country.

Concession seekers kept pressing him, and he feared the Boers of the Transvaal, who wanted land. He held 600 to 800 guns with almost no ammunition. Rudd's party said it wanted only to mine and trade. He reasoned that he would keep his land and gain British protection, and that one powerful holder would end the stream of small prospectors. Younger councillors, the izinDuna, mostly opposed any concession, while older ones were open to it.

The text promised the king £100 every lunar month, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles with 100,000 cartridges, and either a steamboat with guns on the Zambezi River or £500. In return the three men received complete and exclusive charge over all metals and minerals in his lands, and the power to do whatever they judged necessary to get them. The king also authorised them to keep out everyone else seeking land or mining rights, and agreed to grant no more concessions without their consent.

According to the missionary Helm, who interpreted, Rudd promised orally that no more than 10 white men would work in the country, that they would not dig near towns and that they would obey the king's laws. None of that was in the written document, so none of it could be enforced. Helm certified that the terms had been explained to the king and his council. Rhodes called the result so gigantic that it was like giving a man the whole of Australia. The version first published left out the rifles, to avoid alarm among the Boers.

From 1889 Lobengula tried to disown the deal, saying that limits agreed orally had been left out, and sent envoys to Queen Victoria, without success. Britain granted a royal charter to Rhodes's British South Africa Company in October 1889, and the company occupied the neighbouring region of Mashonaland in 1890. The charter gave the company what the paper had never given, the power to govern. Its troops conquered Matabeleland in 1893 and 1894, and Lobengula died in exile soon afterwards. The company's charter ended in 1923, when Southern Rhodesia became a self-governing colony.

A deal limited to minerals thus became the legal foundation for ruling a country.
rudd-concession.mechanism: The written deal covered minerals only and gave no right to rule, but it became the legal basis for a royal charter that let a company annex and govern the country, meaning take it over as its own. The king's objections did not stop it.

ruperts-land-sale.story:
Rupert's Land was a territory of 3.9 million square kilometres around Hudson Bay, about a third of present-day Canada, that a private company held for 200 years. Its origin lies in the fur trade. In the 1660s two French explorers, des Groseilliers and Radisson, saw that Hudson Bay gave an easy water route into the best beaver country. The French government was not interested, so they went to England. A trial voyage in 1668 came back with a large cargo of furs.

King Charles II gave the Hudson's Bay Company a charter in 1670 with exclusive rights to trade and colonise all land whose rivers drained into the bay. The charter took no account of the sovereignty, or right to rule their own land, of the Cree, Assiniboine and other Indigenous peoples living there.

After Canada was formed in 1867, its government wanted the land, partly from fear that the United States, which had just bought Alaska, would take it. The company, for its part, lacked the money to govern a territory that was filling with settlers. It valued the land at up to $40 million, and the United States could have paid that, but Britain would not allow a sale to the Americans and pressed the company to deal with Canada.

After six months of talks the company agreed to £300,000, or about $1.5 million, and kept its trading posts and five per cent of the land, mostly prairie farmland. It was the largest land transaction by area in Canada's history. The company signed the land over to the British Crown on 19 November 1869, and the Crown then ceded it to Canada.

The Red River Resistance, a rising by local people, delayed the transfer until 15 July 1870. Canada then negotiated seven treaties with Indigenous nations to obtain their consent to Crown sovereignty, after the sale and not before. The area was later divided among Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories.
ruperts-land-sale.mechanism: The company could sell only what its charter gave it, so the transfer went through the British Crown to Canada. Indigenous nations were not party to the sale, and Canada made treaties with them afterwards.

sark-fief-sales.story:
Sark, one of the Channel Islands, is a fief, land held from the British monarch, and with the Crown's permission its lordship may be mortgaged or sold. It is on the map because the holder, called the Seigneur, or lord, held governing powers along with the land. In the 1730s a widow, Susanne le Pelley, bought it.

A mortgage is a loan secured on property, and if the borrower stops paying the lender can take the property. In 1844 the Seigneur, Ernest le Pelley, needed money to keep a silver mine running and on 24 February got Crown permission to mortgage the fief for £4,000 to John Allaire, a Guernsey privateer, or licensed ship raider, reputed to be the richest man in Guernsey. Allaire died within two years and his daughter Marie Collings took over the mortgage.

The mine closed in 1847 after its uninsured deepest gallery collapsed, and when Ernest le Pelley died in 1849 the next Seigneur, Pierre Carey le Pelley, could not keep up the payments. When she moved to take the island for the unpaid loan, he asked Queen Victoria's permission to sell on 10 November 1852. On 4 December Collings bought the lordship for £6,000 less the loan and £616 13 shillings of interest, which left £1,383 to pay.

So a lordship with ruling powers passed from one family to another through a failed mining loan, with the Crown's permission needed at each step. She never visited and died the next year. Her family still holds the title. Sark's parliament became fully elected in 2008.
sark-fief-sales.mechanism: A lordship with real governing powers could be bought and sold like property, but only with the monarch's consent, and the monarch stayed overlord throughout.

satoshi-island.story:
Satoshi Island was a plan to turn a private island in Vanuatu, in the South Pacific, into a smart city for cryptocurrency users. Lataro Island is about 3.2 square kilometres of mostly rainforest off the large island of Santo, with a small clearing and one large house. A British entrepreneur, Anthony Welch, had lived there since 2007 under a 75-year lease. Vanuatu appealed to the project partly because of its tax-free income rules.

In 2022 he announced that he would sell plots as NFTs, digital tokens recorded on a blockchain, and aimed at a community of more than 20,000 people in self-powered modular homes. A home package was reported to cost about €100,000 to €120,000. The project spoke of private ownership, but Welch held only a lease, so he could not sell land outright. It spoke of citizenship, but the writer Raymond Craib pointed out that this meant owning one of 21,000 tokens, and buyers would still need a passport to enter Vanuatu. Vanuatu's government said a token gave no right of residence.

The project claimed about 50,000 people had invested, a figure repeated in press reports and not independently confirmed.

In July 2025 the company behind it, Satoshi Island DAO LLC, said all its digital assets could no longer be traded because of a breach of the land lease, citing no real development, no money to keep the site safe and no benefit to local people. Everything sold to buyers rested on that lease. There is no clear evidence that any housing unit was delivered, and its website has gone offline.
satoshi-island.mechanism: Welch held only a lease under Vanuatu law, so token buyers received neither land ownership nor citizenship. The project ended over a breach of that lease.
